entry.title: Congress Must Investigate War Profiteers Once Again

div.p: In April, President Donald Trump requested a $445 billion increase to the defense budget, meaning the United States will be spending around $1.5 trillion on the military. Much of the largesse will benefit the Big Five war contractors: Boeing, General Dynamics, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, and RTX (formerly Raytheon). These are the companies behind such budget-shredding boondoggles as the F-35 and the littoral combat ships.

If the promises of these weapons salesmen are to be believed, the US war with Iran should already be over. The enormousness of the Pentagon’s budget, on paper, means that any conflict the United States enters should be a decidedly short and lopsided affair. Yet Iran has not crumbled against an onslaught that one analyst calculated has cost the United States $72 billion and counting. What has all this spending accomplished?

A US Patriot interceptor missile costs $4 million; a Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptor runs around $13 million. America has fired plenty of both in the war with Iran. Contrast that with the Iranian attack drones these systems are meant to shoot down, which run anywhere from $20,000 to $50,000 apiece. These swarms of cheap drones are able to effectively counter US aircraft carriers whose price tags run into the billions (that is, when laundry room fires don’t do the job). The United States has fired off so much ordnance that talk has turned to a possible missile shortage.

All this weaponry comes at a steep price for the average American back home. In April, a report from the Institute for Policy Studies found that the average taxpayer spends approximately $4,000 per year on war and weaponry. What is all this money going toward? Who has really benefited from over a trillion dollars a year in annual military spending? In a spirit sorely lacking today, Congress tried to answer these and other questions ninety years ago when it forthrightly challenged the Pentagon and military contractors in its famous Nye Committee of 1934.

header.h2: The Big, Corrupt Business of Arms Sales

div.p: In the wake of the Great Depression, a wave of anti-militarism and anti–weapons manufacturer sentiment swept the United States. Books like Iron, Blood, and Profits by muckraker George Seldes and the bestseller Merchants of Death by H. C. Engelbrecht and F. C. Hanighen exposed the workings of the international arms trade. Even Fortune, no hotbed of radicalism then or now, published its own exposé, “Arms and the Men,” which was reprinted for a wider audience in Reader’s Digest.

A shocked public demanded action. Dorothy Detzer of the Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom approached Nebraska Senator George Norris about launching a Senate investigation into the munitions industry. Norris was a natural choice given that he had strongly opposed World War I, arguing the country was “going into war upon the command of gold. We are going to run the risk of sacrificing millions of our countrymen’s lives in order that other countrymen may coin their lifeblood into money.” But Norris begged off, citing illness and overwork.

Instead Norris suggested North Dakota’s Gerald Nye. Although a Republican, he was supported by the left-wing Nonpartisan League. Nye was a firm anti-militarist who condemned Uncle Sam for “helping to crucify” the people of Nicaragua via military interventions to shore up business interests. Nye had already served on two Senate investigations and was picked to chair the two-year inquiry.

The Special Committee on Investigation of the Munitions Industry, commonly referred to as the Nye Committee, uncovered some explosive evidence: arms manufacturers frequently bribed officials. Clarence Webster of Curtiss-Wright Export Corporation objected to the “rather harsh” term “bribery” before admitting that the greasing of palms was employed, “strictly speaking.”

Curtiss-Wright played countries against one another for profit, telling one sales representative in Peru during the Colombia-Peru War to “diplomatically inform interested parties that your neighbor to the extreme north [Colombia] is still purchasing large quantities. Do not overlook such items as bombs, ammunition, machine guns equipment, etc.” They were not alone.

A Colt salesman explained to the Bolivian consul that “it would be advisable for [Bolivia] to act quickly if [it] wanted to get these guns, intimating that a certain other government might get them if Bolivia did not act quickly.” The Paraguayan government was the other party, then fighting Bolivia in the Chaco War.

Frank Jonas of Remington Arms proclaimed during the war: “The unsettled conditions in South America [have] been a great thing for me, as I sold a large order for bombs to Brazil and also a fair cartridge order. I also sold very large bomb orders for Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia.”

Arms manufacturers complained of US diplomatic efforts that might put a damper on business. A representative of Electric Boat (today a part of General Dynamics) complained to a counterpart from Vickers (today a part of UK defense contractor BAE Systems), “It is too bad that the pernicious activities of our State Department have put the brake on armament orders.” Peace, it seems, was just too unprofitable.

It even turned out that a commander in the US Navy was moonlighting as an arms salesman. James H. Strong helped peddle the wares of two munitions makers and received a tidy commission for doing so. Nye was shocked to find “governments — especially our own war and navy departments — have been actively promoting the munitions-makers, for years.”

The committee also investigated the sky-high profits arms manufacturers had made during World War I. DuPont, headed by one of the oldest and richest families in America, saw an increase in its profits of 1,130 percent. Eugene Grace, president of Bethlehem Steel, testified to how “unfortunate” it was that Bonus Marchers had marched on Washington to protest for their World War I bonuses. He then admitted, with no seeming sense of irony, that he had received almost $3 million in bonuses during the war. The situation, he averred, could “leave a bad taste” in veterans’ mouths.

Shocking revelations aside, the Nye Committee produced little substantial legislation. Efforts to nationalize the arms manufacturers failed despite widespread public support, as did a campaign to require a national referendum before declaring war. The Neutrality Acts that did result were whittled away as the country moved back on a war footing in the lead-up to the attack on Pearl Harbor. In his farewell address, Nye said he was “more proud of having” led the Senate inquiry than of anything else in his career.

header.h2: Under Trump, War Is More Profitable Than Ever

div.p: Recent books like The Trillion Dollar War Machine by William D. Hartung and Ben Freeman and The Spoils of War by Andrew Cockburn have followed the trail blazed by Engelbrecht, Hanighen, and Seldes. The authors have documented the revolving door between military contractors, government, and think tanks; the corrosive effects of arms-industry and foreign lobbying; and efforts to influence the media. The merchants of death are still on their bad behavior. In January 2025, a citizens’ tribunal found that American weapons contractors are themselves guilty of crimes against humanity, including genocide. Open briery — “rather harsh” or not — has not disappeared, as Raytheon’s recent legal troubles have proven.

Conflicts of interest and public officials acting as salesmen for private arms manufacturers are also still with us. Palmer Luckey of Anduril Industries is both a major Trump donor dating back to 2016 and a recipient of Pentagon liberality, with his company receiving a $250 million contract to produce missiles and drones for the military. Luckey has suggested the United States needs to “hyperscale manufacturing” for a potential showdown with China, ideally (and conveniently) with his company’s Arsenal-1 weapons factory in Ohio. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has pushed for a Pentagon shake-up to better facilitate the overseas arms trade. Even the president’s sons Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump have positioned themselves for a windfall through their investments in various companies manufacturing military drones. Ninety years later, General Smedley Butler’s war racket continues to make a killing, regardless of how unpopular a war like the one in Iran might be. It’s a big, well-armed club, and we aren’t in it.

“Investigations serve a most healthy purpose,” Nye said, the year before chairing the committee. “With economics and political influence coming into such concentrated control it is of greatest importance that legislative bodies be on closest guard against encroachment which further threatens a free government. . . . We should have not less, but more legislative investigations.”

The issues raised by his investigation have only worsened in the intervening years. After the boondoggles of Iraq, Afghanistan, and now Iran, the time has come for a twenty-first-century Nye Committee. If we don’t act, those wars — no matter how unpopular — will grind on. There’s simply too much money to be made.

entry.title: Bernie Sanders’s 2016 Campaign Lit a Spark Beyond Elections

div.p: Bernie Sanders’s impact on the American left is not typically measured in social movement terms. The story normally goes that democratic socialism returned to national politics after 2015, tens of thousands of people joined the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a new generation of socialist candidates ran for office, and a much larger left media ecosystem emerged.
That’s all true. But another part of the story has received relatively less attention: the role Bernie’s campaigns played in inspiring and cohering a new generation of labor activists.

I first started making this argument while writing about the red-state teachers’ revolt of 2018. Obviously, Bernie did not cause these massive statewide strikes; years of austerity and attacks on public education created the conditions. But while reporting on those strikes on the ground in West Virginia, Oklahoma, and Arizona, I kept finding that many of the rank-and-file leaders who took the initiative to get them started had been politicized by Bernie’s 2016 campaign.

“The role of the Bernie campaign of 2016 on organizing in West Virginia really cannot be overstated,” Charleston teacher and strike leader Emily Comer told me. Bernie’s campaign, she explained, “got people, especially young people, plugged in who before had been feeling hopeless and who would not have made their way into organizing before.”

This was not just retrospective speculation. Morgantown teacher Anna Simmons described the night West Virginia teachers decided to defy their unions’ proposed settlement and continue their strike. It was the moment, she told me, when she realized that the fight “was about more than just insurance premiums and salaries. It was the continuation of a movement that started with Bernie Sanders and is going to result in a power shift from the elite wealthy to the working people.”
When I first made this case about the 2018 strikes, some critics dismissed it as a Bernie Bro exaggeration. But what happened after 2020 made the larger pattern much harder to dismiss.

The post-pandemic labor upsurge has been driven to an unusual degree by young workers organizing from below, many of whom were radicalized and made class conscious by Bernie. For my book We Are the Union, I surveyed over two thousand worker leaders who unionized their workplaces in 2022; the median respondent was twenty-seven years old and almost half identified politically as radicals.

When I asked what broader movements had influenced them, recent labor struggles were, unsurprisingly, the biggest factor. Yet more than 80 percent of respondents cited at least one outside struggle as a major influence on their decision to unionize. Among non-labor movements, Black Lives Matter and Bernie stood out: BLM had the widest reach, followed right behind by Bernie, whose campaigns also had the most intense reported impact.

My interviews with worker leaders put faces on those numbers. Max Yusen, who helped turn his St Louis Starbucks into a union stronghold, had not grown up around organized labor. “Labor was a big part of Bernie’s message,” he told me, “and being around union members while canvassing and inside DSA really made me see how important they are.” When he moved back to St Louis, he deliberately got a job at Starbucks “with the goal of unionizing it.”

Bernie’s influence also produced institutions that outlasted his campaigns. The Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee (EWOC) grew directly out of Bernie 2020 and the DSA for Bernie campaign. When Covid hit in March 2020, workers began contacting the Sanders campaign asking for help winning protective equipment and sick pay. A handful of labor organizers from the campaign, along with organizers from DSA and the United Electrical Workers, set up a Google form and began connecting those workers with volunteer organizers. It was, from the start, animated by both the class-struggle politics and the distributed organizing model of the Sanders campaign.

The same political generation appeared elsewhere in the post-2020 upsurge. Most of the salts, the rank-and-file workers who got jobs in order to organize and who played an important role in the successful Amazon Labor Union campaign at JFK8 on Staten Island had been politicized by Bernie’s presidential runs. At Starbucks, Amazon, CVS, Trader Joe’s, and elsewhere, young workers entered organizing with an anti-billionaire politics that had become far more widespread since 2016.

None of this means that Bernie produced the labor upsurge. Covid was a huge catalyst. So was the tight labor market, a more favorable National Labor Relations Board under President Joe Biden, digital tools, and, above all, the contagious example of workers themselves winning. The 2018 teachers’ strikes themselves helped inspire later strikes; Starbucks and Amazon victories then convinced thousands of other workers that organizing was possible.

But recent evidence does make the connection I saw in 2018 look less incidental. Electoral campaigns can feed workplace struggle by politicizing people, raising their expectations, bringing activists together, and giving them experience organizing others. Bernie’s campaigns did all four.

And that story is still unfolding. Amazon organizing has expanded far beyond the original JFK8 victory: the Teamsters reported this year that roughly ten thousand Amazon workers had organized at thirteen facilities around the country. In New York, Amazon workers and Teamsters are simultaneously organizing on the job and campaigning for the Delivery Protection Act, which would regulate last-mile facilities and impose new employment and safety requirements; as of September 2026, the bill remains pending in the city council with thirty-five council sponsors.

Once MAGA is ejected from the White House, there is every reason to expect that the Bernie generation of labor organizers will go back on the offensive nationwide to unionize the megacorporations that have reaped the benefits of America’s New Gilded Age and that, virtually without exception, have bent the knee to Donald Trump.

Bernie’s contribution to the revival of the American left, then, did not stop with DSA or socialist electoral politics. As Vince Quiles, a young Home Depot worker in Philadelphia, put it to me: “Bernie showed me and a lot of people my age that it’s not a bad thing to fight corporations or demand more from your government. We’re workers, you know, we produce everything, and we deserve more.”

entry.title: US Meddling in Brazil May Decide Latin America’s Future

div.p: As Brazil heads toward Sunday’s presidential election first round, the contest is on a knife-edge. Polls show left-wing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva neck and neck with the ultraconservative Flávio Bolsonaro, the oldest of his imprisoned father’s brood.

Jair Bolsonaro was defeated in 2022, as was the subsequent attempted coup that led to his criminal conviction. (He is now under house arrest.) Still, Bolsonarismo remained a powerful force. Compared to the high drama of four years ago, this campaign has at times seemed subdued, in part because most other candidates essentially offer duller, more gray-haired versions of Bolsonarismo.

And yet the stakes couldn’t be higher. Not only is Brazilian democracy again on the line, but the region more widely is increasingly subject to right-wing authoritarians in thrall to Donald Trump and Marco Rubio. Brazil is for now an exception, along with Mexico — that is, Latin America’s two largest economies and most populous countries.

If Brazil does follow the recent right-wing trend, the region’s future is grim. US intervention in favor of Flávio Bolsonaro has been brazen; Brazil’s national intelligence agency, ABIN, has presented evidence of meddling ranging from “from lawfare to interference that is openly acknowledged.” It is not the only factor, but it is making itself felt.

While Lula’s third stint in government has offered a sense of normality and economic gains for Brazil’s working class, his agenda has been hamstrung by the most right-wing Congress in Brazilian history. He has been held back by three main forces — the so-called Bible (evangelical), Beef (agribusiness) and Bullet (military/police) lobbies.

Lula’s third term has had its achievements: above-inflation increases in the minimum wage, healthy growth, and expanding social security, plus historically low levels of unemployment. But he hasn’t had a singular major policy win of the kind that led to him leaving office in 2010 with an 80 percent-plus approval rate. While most Brazilians are technically better off than four years ago, the cost of living is higher, as are levels of indebtedness; four-fifths of Brazilian families are in debt, in part driven by the social cancer of online gambling. Jobs are increasingly precarious, and public security remains a key drama; though violent crime is down, rampant phone theft and extraordinarily high levels of online scamming make crime a daily concern for millions.

After Jair Bolsonaro was convicted and sentenced to twenty-seven years in prison, along with several major allies, it seemed as if the leadership of the Brazilian right was up for grabs. However, the power of Bolsonarismo became clear as soon as Flávio announced he was running. All the other major contenders, like São Paulo Governor Tarcísio de Freitas, dropped out of the equation. Flávio also blocked the potential candidacy of his stepmother Michelle, who has built a large and especially female evangelical base; she offered a tepid endorsement only after public squabbles with her stepson.

Even for seasoned Brazil watchers, it has been hard to reckon with the possibility that this country might soon elect its version of Jackie Aprile Junior, whose main goal is to free his father. Still Flávio, dubbed “01” by Jair, a typical mobbed-up Rio politician, has styled himself as more moderate than his father and is also the relatively normal one in the Bolsonaro clan. He is more normal, at least, compared to his deranged troll brother Carlos (“02”), a Senate candidate who happens to have a tattoo of his dad’s face on his arm; or the self-exiled former Congressman Eduardo (“03”) who, after losing his seat due to prolonged absences, has been lobbying from Texas for Trump to impose sanctions on Brazil.

This is an election perhaps best defined by “apathetic polarization,” to use Brian Winter’s phrase, where policy or future vision is secondary to passive distaste for the candidates. In the right-wing camp this especially means a widespread anti–Workers’ Party (PT) sentiment known as anti-petismo, in which Lula’s party is blamed for all of Brazil’s ills and even right-wingers’ personal troubles.

To paraphrase Celso Rocha de Barros, one of Brazil’s leading public intellectuals: Flávio is a stand-in for various sinister interests — the gambling lobby, banking fraudsters, imperial Miami, organized crime, and social-security scammers. His program mostly consists of law-and-order bromides about chemical castration for rapists — slightly complicated by the fact that his running mate has been accused of raping a minor — and constructing five megaprisons. However, his real program is basically about handing over Brazil’s critical minerals and sovereignty to Trump and Rubio in order to free his dad.

Lula’s campaign has picked up some momentum in the final stages of the campaign. One smart move was to ban Brazil’s largely unregulated and highly exploitative online sports betting and casino apps, modeled after cellphone games called tigrinho, and known colloquially as “bets.” Gambling was legalized under Bolsonaro and has had a devastating effect on working-class life; his ex–Chicago Boy finance minister, Paulo Guedes, infamously remarked, “Let everyone f–k themselves over” at a cabinet meeting deciding on the move. Lula is also seeking to change the country’s employment code from “6 x 1” (six days of work, one day off) to a two-day weekend.

The fact that this election remains a coin toss is in part due to a familiar pattern of frustration with the incumbent. Still, that doesn’t explain how Flávio has a real chance of victory, given his own lack of personal appeal, his connection to almost every corruption scandal and organized crime group in Brazil, as is the fact that his father is in prison for an attempted coup, not to mention the previous Bolsonaro government’s disastrous response to COVID, which actively contributed to the death toll of over seven hundred thousand. Something deeper and more paradigmatic is going on, reflecting the fragmentation of Brazilian society under late neoliberalism and the destructive effects of the attention economy.

As Rodrigo Nunes, author of a new tour de force on the global right, puts it in a recent interview with Equator magazine, in Brazil we see both a “hyper-individualisation of politics and the privileging of online participation over offline organising. It profoundly shapes how most of the contemporary far right is organised: as a sort of pyramid scheme whose building blocks are ‘political entrepreneurs’ — people who, from a position of prominence on social or traditional media, produce content that at once accrues attentional, social and political capital.”
Still, while this reflects deep shifts in Brazilian society, there is also a cruder force at work: US interference.

As Piero Locatelli writes, this is a country where businessmen openly “admit on podcasts that they are part of U.S. networks that work with Brazilian campaigns” also because “firms linked to Donald Trump, Jr (as well as J. D. Vance) invest in the extraction of rare earth minerals here.”

Naturally, for analysts — in Brazil and internationally — conditioned to viewing claims of US intervention as vulgar or conspiratorial, it has been hard to process the reality and significance of meddling and dark ops in this election. Even most left-wingers tend to point toward the significance of material factors rather than CIA hijinks. Still, in an election with such close margins, US intervention really may be decisive, as we have already seen in Peru, Colombia, and Honduras, where right-wingers won with less than 1 percent advantage.

Now even The New York Times is calling out US electoral interference. Last week, thirty members of Congress, including Bernie Sanders, wrote a letter declaring that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy,” the United States was “acting as an agent of interference and destabilization — using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions” and even hurting a strategic US ally. This week, Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Tim Kaine, and Peter Welch asked Rubio if the administration will recognize the election results if it doesn’t go Flávio’s way. Rubio is, predictably, yet to respond.

Some of these measures are overt, such as Trump tweeting endorsements or threatening Latin American leaders with the “Venezuela option.” He does so either by pointing a metaphorical gun to their heads via X or providing major financial aid, like the $20 billion to help out Argentinian President Javier Milei in the local elections, and the recent suspension of all consular services in Brazil on the eve of the elections.

Perhaps the most dangerous move was designating Brazil’s two largest criminal factions, Rio’s Comando Vermelho (CV) and São Paulo’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) as narcoterrorist organizations despite them having negligible, if any, presence in the United States. This classification potentially opens the door to unilateral military strikes on suspected narcoterrorists within Brazil’s borders. Through the recently launched Shield of Americas initiative, Trump’s willing vassals followed suit in classifying the CV and PCC as narcoterrorists at a meeting held during the United Nations’ General Assembly.

Other approaches are more covert. One senior Brazilian cyber official told Reuters that ​“the number of cyberattacks in Brazil had nearly doubled compared with 2025” combined with a sharp increase “in hacks and phishing attempts of the president’s office,” which the official said was clearly election-related. This week’s revelations include a Trump-funded influence campaign against Brazil’s Supreme Court.

We have also been offered a window into the sheer scale and depravity of the political fixers and influence peddlers that make regular journeys between Mar-a-Lago and Latin American capitals in the case of a particularly sleazy Argentinian named Fernando Cerimedo. He has been described by the Economist as MAGA’s man in America, whose sordid dealings came to light after he allegedly ordered a (failed) hit on his pregnant girlfriend in Bolivia. He is also charged with protecting cocaine shipments for a fee heading to Brazil, presumably to “narcoterrorists”; Cerimedo made his bones working on the 2022 Bolsonaro campaign pushing pro-coup narratives and has close ties to the family; he claims to have befriended Eduardo at Harvard (which neither of them attended). This week, on orders from Rubio, Bolivia arrested the man looking into the Cerimedo affair, Attorney General Roger Mariaca, two days after the United States revoked his visa, accusing him of the same charges facing Cerimedo. This move, in turn, was applauded in an official statement from the Shield of the Americas.

There is even a segment of Bolsonaro supporters who have a perverse fantasy of Trump invading the country and eliminating the Left once and for all; “Come soon, Trump, do what you did in Venezuela. The decent Brazilian supports you,” as Mario Rey of São Paulo wrote in a letter published by Folha de São Paulo, Brazil’s paper of record.

header.h2: The Endless Pitfalls of Anti-Corruption Politics

div.p: This campaign has also been defined by the largest banking fraud in Brazilian history, in which Banco Master’s CEO Daniel Vorcaro allegedly operated a $10 billion pyramid scheme by buying off much of Brazil’s elite, including at least five members of the Supreme Court. They were allegedly won over with $8,000 bottles of whiskey, investments in the companies of justices’ relatives, and private parties featuring the likes of Swedish House Mafia and Flo Rida at São Paulo clubs, with a carefully curated selection of international young female company.

Due to the role of the Supreme Court — in particular Justice Alexandre de Moraes — in prosecuting Jair Bolsonaro and making inquiries into his disinformation machine, there is an ongoing perception that the court is allied with the Left, rather than simply acting in self-interest in a way that on occasion aligns with Brazilian democracy. This same court, after all, blocked Lula from running in 2018. As a result, the ongoing scandal has been more damaging for Lula than Flávio, despite the latter hitching rides on Vorcaro’s private plane and soliciting $28.2million for the most expensive film in Brazilian history, a biopic of Jair starring Jim Caviezel titled Dark Horse. Despite the cash, this film does not have a release date, and the only footage ever released was taken down from X after Beyoncé sued the production for using the song “Survivor” without her permission.

As I have argued in Jacobin, anti-corruption politics can lead to “a cycle of diminishing expectations, producing apathy and political demoralization.” In spreading the idea that politics is merely a game of sordid self-interest in which the powerful collude to loot the public purse, it undermines the bases of collective action.

It is a tragic irony that much of the electorate most concerned about organized crime backs a candidate who is himself so close to the Rio de Janeiro mafia, who is backed by the online betting lobby, and whose best friend stands accused of embezzling over a billion dollars through social security fraud. Flávio is personally tied to the killers of Rio socialist city councilor Marielle Franco in more ways than one. He is also the owner of dozens of high-end properties, including a multimillion-dollar beachfront mansion he managed to seize through his political and legal power from Tottenham striker Richarlison, an impressive feat for a man officially earning a salary of around $8,900.

Crime and public security have largely been a weakness for the Left in Latin America and elsewhere, with a widespread perception that it is soft on criminals or even in league with organized crime. It has been the dominant narrative in the Right’s recent electoral victories (and authoritarian crackdowns) in countries like Ecuador, Peru, and Colombia. This even when the performative ironfisted strongman candidates seem to have deep ties to organized crime and promote security policies that have been tried, tested, and failed for over three decades.

The problem is that moral outrage and pointing out the hypocrisy have proven to be a remarkably ineffective political response for left-wing candidates. The fact is that investing in social disintegration is both an effective political strategy for Latin America’s new right and a means for imperial Miami under Trump and Rubio to assert their dominance over Latin America. All that can be said, hopefully, is that the die has not yet been cast, and Lula could still repel Miami’s invasion of Brazil through the Trojan Horse that is Flávio Bolsonaro.

entry.title: The Battle of Cable Street Was an Antifascist Landmark

div.p: Twenty years ago, I shared a platform with Aubrey Morris, one of the “ordinary” heroes of the Battle of Cable Street on October 4, 1936 — the iconic event in Britain’s prewar antifascist history. Aubrey was sixteen at the time, a Labour League of Youth member, and he still glowed with pride at having been part of the mass defiance that put the slogan “They shall not pass” into spectacular effect. He helped build barricades in Cable Street.

Aubrey denied being a hero: “I did what any young Jewish boy would have done at that time.” Though he did have an additional motive. If Oswald Mosley’s uniformed, jackbooted British Union of Fascists (BUF) had invaded that narrow street to terrorize its largely Jewish residents, they would have reached number 86, where Aubrey’s grandmother ran the family’s bagel bakery! He took this personally.

Eventually, police partially dislodged the first barricade — a tipped-over truck with furniture stacked behind it, blocking the road. They ran through to find a route for the fascists to march but got trapped between that truck and the next barricade. There they faced fierce resistance at ground level and an aerial barrage of objects thrown by women in flats above the shops.

The antifascist mobilization that day in Cable Street and the surrounding area stands out for its extraordinary scale and the powerful psychological blow it dealt to Mosley’s British Union of Fascists at a time when fascist parties were making gains across Europe.

Mosley repeatedly told his followers that they were “invincible.” But a week later, he acknowledged that they had been “humiliated” in East London. This Sunday, October 4, we will be marching again from Tower Hamlets Town Hall to Cable Street to mark the nineteenth anniversary of this landmark.

Those defending the Jewish end of Cable Street on the day were reinforced by dockers from the street’s largely Irish Limehouse end. A propaganda battle raged for the allegiances of the Irish locals. Mosley won over a segment of them, gaining recruits who frequently delivered antisemitic tirades on street-corner fascist platforms.

But antifascists were patiently building a class-based unity between Jews and Irish against Mosley that recalled a history of unity and solidarity between tailors and dockers in strikes. The Communist Party prepared special “Speakers Notes” for use in Irish areas, reminding audiences of the unjust discrimination and scapegoating their community suffered over decades. On October 4, 1936, many Irish defended Cable Street alongside Jews.

Joyce Rosenthal was younger than Aubrey, just twelve when she and a friend joined the mass blockade at Gardiner’s Corner, Aldgate, half a mile north of Cable Street. Mosley planned to lead his troops from Royal Mint Street, in the City of London, to Gardiner’s, before marching through the heart of Jewish Whitechapel.

After that, they were to split into four columns, tramping through Jewish-populated streets toward platforms being erected by Mosley’s local fascist branches — in Shoreditch, Bethnal Green, Bow, and Limehouse — for open-air victory meetings. Mosley, “The Leader,” promised to address each one.

However, the blockade at Gardiner’s was so dense that it withstood repeated charges by truncheon-wielding mounted police. The police relayed a message to Mosley, in Royal Mint Street, to say that he would not reach Gardiner’s but would have to enter further south. The antifascists predicted that the police would use Cable Street.
Youngsters like Aubrey were already erecting barricades there. The entrance to Cable Street saw some of the fiercest fighting that day between police and antifascists, and many arrests.

After Mosley was beaten back at Cable Street too, the police eventually instructed him to turn his troops around, head west to Embankment and disperse. Mosley accused the police of surrendering to “red and Jewish terror,” but he complied. He was due in Berlin two days later to marry Diana Mitford, in Adolf Hitler’s presence and at the home of Nazi Minister of Propaganda Joseph Goebbels.

Demonstrators were jubilant as the fascists scurried westward, though the seventy-nine antifascists arrested on the day, many of whom were severely beaten at Leman Street police station, were probably feeling more subdued. Just five fascists were arrested that afternoon.

The police had mobilized seven thousand officers to facilitate four thousand fascist marchers after the home secretary rejected a petition to ban the march that had collected nearly a hundred thousand signatures. The Jewish People’s Council Against Fascism and Antisemitism (JPC), a radical grassroots Jewish campaign formed in July 1936, drafted the petition. The home secretary justified his decision to allow the march citing “free speech” and “free movement” (for the fascists), prioritizing their freedoms over community fears.

The Jewish community’s West End–based “leaders,” the Board of Deputies and Anglo-Jewish Association, held themselves aloof from the anger brewing in the East End’s working-class Jewish streets. They told Jews to stay indoors and asked rabbis to deliver synagogue sermons driving home that message twenty-four hours before the battle.

The Jewish Chronicle newspaper, a reliable cheerleader for representatives of the Jewish elite, warned Jews to “keep away from the route of the Blackshirt march,” adding that if Jews “become involved in any possible disorders,” they would be “actively helping antisemitism.”

But they were not the ones feeling the heat. As Charlie Goodman, who served three months in prison after Cable Street, told me: “The fascists rant against rich Jews in Park Lane then beat up a Jew in Brick Lane,” the famous East End street.

Charlie recalled the transparent tactic employed by Jewish youth club directors locally, who organized additional football matches that Sunday to divert youngsters from protesting. The youth chose to tackle fascism that day rather than tackle each other on a football pitch.
After the war, Charlie married Joyce Rosenthal. She asked him an important question before agreeing to their first date: “Where were you on October 4?”

By and large, the East End Jews, who experienced daily antisemitic abuse and assaults from fascists through 1936, ignored the advice of their communal establishment. They responded energetically to the JPC’s leaflets, which were distributed hours after the home secretary rejected their petition.

Addressed to “Citizens of London,” the leaflets stated: “This March Must Not Take Place!” If the government wouldn’t ban it, the people would. Estimates of numbers on the streets opposing the fascists on October 4, 1936, range from one hundred thousandto three hundred thousand.

The established political organizations that were already campaigning against fascism in several ways — especially the Communist Party (CP), the Independent Labour Party (ILP) and the Labour League of Youth (LLY) — echoed the JPC’s call. The CP recruited strongly among East End Jews in this period, on issues of poverty, unemployment, and housing as well as antifascism. CP activists were well represented within the broad-based JPC, which was supported by local synagogues, youth and student groups, Jewish trade unions, community associations, and friendly societies.

When antifascists today look for inspiration on how to effectively oppose and stop Britain’s contemporary far right, they are drawn instinctively toward the blockades and barricades of the most dramatic physical confrontations. Cable Street was by far the largest, but between 1933 and 1938, people also united in numbers seeking to deny the streets to the fascists in many other towns and cities: Aberdeen, Bristol, Hull, Leeds, Liverpool, Manchester, Oxford, Stockton, Tonypandy, and the seaside town of Worthing.

These local antifascist uprisings form a single constellation, and they should all be celebrated. The skills that activists honed in building and organizing mass mobilizations, decades before they could share pinned locations on social media, remain astonishing.

Today, when the Left is riven with sectarianism and its own destructive versions of cancel culture, we should seek to emulate the inclusivity of 1930s antifascist protests. These were based on unity in action without demanding uniformity of thought, though there were, of course, theorists analyzing the growth of fascism around Europe, who it was attracting, and how that process could be interrupted.

It is vital, though, to recognize that these local antifascist battles were reactive. The fascists had seized the agenda by threatening to invade specific areas. By doing so, they sought to intimidate those they perceived as their enemies, but also to recruit members (including the unemployed) who might be impressed by their propaganda and their militaristic style, which conveyed a sense of unity and power.

The JPC believed that antifascists needed to assert their own broader strategy, patiently building antifascist majorities in local areas across the divisions the fascists sought to impose. They embodied this approach in their public meetings, which always had both Jewish and non-Jewish speakers on the platform.

The global economic crash of 1929 created the crisis that opened the doors to fascism. Many countries suffered high unemployment rates through that decade, fostering a growing sense of hopelessness. In Britain, there was a widespread belief that the “tired old gang” of politicians — as Mosley dubbed Conservative, Liberal, and Labour leaders in Britain — had created dire economic problems that they could not resolve.

Mosley was in his mid-thirties when he launched the British Union of Fascists (BUF). He described his movement as a “party of action based on youth that would mobilize energy, vitality and manhood to save and rebuild the nation.” His opportunistic use of generational politics and his emphasis on “the nation” obscured his own superwealthy economic position and the class interests he represented and sought to defend.

This deceptive approach helped him win cross-class political support. Young people — and many of their parents too — were drawn to Mosley’s antiwar rhetoric. He claimed that his party alone offered young people opportunities to serve the nation in peacetime, not just as war fodder. Dig deeper, and you will find the youth he was really interested in: BUF-supporting student societies in twenty elite public schools, grooming the next generation of fascist ideologues.

Far-right parties and movements in today’s Britain naturally exploit the cost-of-living crisis. But when younger left-wing activists shift the blame to “boomers,” I weep. I think of working-class communities, especially in northern England and Wales, where so many people’s lives were devastated in the 1980s as Margaret Thatcher waged war on trade unions and industries closed down. Yes, a section of people got rich in that decade, but most working-class “boomers” were left impoverished and leading precarious lives. They still do.

From autumn 1934, the BUF promoted a virulent form of antisemitism that attempted to explain every social, political, and economic problem as resulting from “alien Yiddish finance.” Mosley found support for antisemitism in every social class. Antisemitic stereotypes of Jews as alien, cunning, evil, and manipulative were commonplace in the 1920s, molded into conspiracy theories that posited a worldwide threat from “Judeo-Bolshevism.”

This kind of antisemitism slipped effortlessly from the tongues of Tory politicians and right-wing newspaper publishers, filtering downward. This is worth reflecting on when we consider how the normalization of Islamophobia within mainstream society over the last twenty-five years has boosted Britain’s current far-right forces, who try to blame every problem on migrants and refugees.

Whenever Mosley announced that the BUF would march in a particular area, people at the grassroots came together to discuss how to respond, with local trade unions and left-wing parties — especially the CP and ILP — in the forefront. While successful resistance was not guaranteed, fascist plans were often disrupted at the very least. In some cases, the fascists were literally chased out of town. In others, both sides later claimed victory.

If we are going to draw important lessons from the 1930s for activists today, we also have to examine the breadth of the work they undertook during that decade in the period between mobilizations. We also need to analyze the different elements that comprised the fascist threat, how the fascists were able to recruit in different localities, and what made people vulnerable to being recruited by fascism. This is the kind of analysis that makes it possible to draw some people away from the far right and even to bring them into a collective struggle for better lives for all.

The activist-theorists of the 1930s distinguished between two aspects of the problem they were facing. On the one hand, there was fascism as a sophisticated, totalizing ideology, adhered to by a growing core of educated far-right actors in Britain and across Europe. On the other hand, there was a larger number of individuals drawn toward the fascist flag by a sense that their circumstances were rapidly deteriorating and that no one was on their side. Mosley’s party offered them a chance to be part of something new that could restore their pride as well as providing them with someone to blame for their problems.

The activists did not simply write off people who reacted positively to what Mosley said (still less disparage them as “scum”). They viewed them as people who could be persuaded by a different set of ideas, a vision of a better future, especially if it simultaneously showed them where and how they could play a part themselves in bringing about change.

In 2026, we need to think more creatively about how to stem the growth of the far right and the normalization of their ideology — including crude and violent racism today — beyond a fixation with outnumbering them at every protest opportunity, however small. We need to be more strategic and not use the same tactics for every situation.

A few days after the Battle of Cable Street, Mosley went looking for revenge. The fascists mobilized a counterprotest against a victory march from Bethnal Green to Tower Hill that was organized by antifascist ex-servicemen. The marchers faced horrific antisemitic abuse at close quarters, not to mention physical attacks with razor blades and other weapons. However, this was a decoy maneuver.

While police focused on containing that counterprotest, another group of fascists, 150-strong, mainly teenagers, ran riot a mile away, between Stepney Green and Mile End. They set fire to cars and attacked Jewish-owned shops, beating shopkeepers who fought back with wooden planks. A hair salon owner and a young child were thrown through a plate glass window. The fascists also launched an assault on the residents of a predominantly Jewish housing block.

Immediately after Cable Street, Mosley’s party recruited hundreds of youngsters seeking the excitement of physical action, but they got bored quickly. More serious fights raged within Mosley’s inner circle, where formerly devoted admirers now became hypercritical. Some resigned; some even defected over the coming months to the antifascists — and were rightly welcomed.

Mosley saw the spring 1937 local elections as an opportunity to revive the party’s agitational work. They stood candidates in their three strongest East End areas, Bethnal Green, Shoreditch, and Limehouse, promising local supporters they would win. Their highest vote was 23 percent in Bethnal Green, whereas Labour candidates in those seats won with more than 60 percent of the vote.

Predictably, Mosley blamed Jews for voting Labour as a bloc, though each of these seats was on the margins of the local Jewish enclave and there were in fact few Jewish voters. But many Jewish activists, especially those mobilized by the JPC, went there to leaflet, canvass, and urge people not to vote for fascists. Non-Jewish antifascists did so too. Effectively it was the non-Jewish voters who defeated Mosley, having been convinced by antifascist arguments. This victory, which was as important as Cable Street, was achieved in a very different manner.

In summer 1937, another antifascist opportunity presented itself. It involved a grassroots campaign that mushroomed in 1938–39, bringing the very communities that the fascists had sought to divide into close cooperative contact and delivering real gains for ordinary people, while making the area much less hospitable for fascists. Phil Piratin, a Jewish communist, was prominent in this campaign.

Piratin had been born into a Ukrainian Jewish family in Whitechapel. The CP recruited him as a member in 1934 through the antifascist struggle, when he was twenty-seven years old. He was very worried about the growth of the fascists locally and across Europe and grappled with the question of why the poorest people locally were drawn to the aristocrat Mosley and his party.

As a Jew, Piratin was sensitive about antisemitism, but he didn’t think that was the principal driver. In his view, unemployment, poor wages, and appalling housing conditions were more significant in pulling struggling people toward a dynamic political alternative. He urged the CP to work energetically on these issues, convinced that this would enhance their direct campaigning against fascists.

The party began working among tenants on local estates in the East End’s Stepney area, out of which the Stepney Tenants Defence League (STDL) was formed. In June 1937, Piratin learned that two families in rent arrears in Paragon Mansions, Stepney Green faced imminent eviction. One family had five children, the other six.

They were reluctant to accept help from the League, which they associated with communists. Both families were BUF members. But Piratin knew he should persist. One family soon came on board; the other did so later and more reluctantly. A campaign that involved barricading the estate and beating off bailiffs was successful.

Piratin asked the families what the BUF had done for them to help. They couldn’t answer. The tenants stayed, settled their arrears, and tore up their BUF membership cards. The League produced a leaflet, widely circulated, that showed what tenants could do when they united across the dividing lines the fascists encouraged.

This was the spur to a broader ongoing campaign that saw more than twenty successful local rent strikes between August 1938 and the summer of 1939. These strikes won concrete gains for renters and brought together people from different communities, especially Irish and Jewish tenants. Women from both communities did much of the day-to-day organizational work. Tenants paid a small weekly subscription to join the STDL.

At the time of the Battle of Cable Street, the most organized radical left-wing force locally, the Communists, had around a thousand members in Stepney, including the party’s youth section. By the middle of 1939, the STDL, instigated by communists but reaching much more widely, had around eleven thousand members. This movement cemented the victory at Cable Street and made longer-term gains for working-class communities.

In our work today, organizing in our localities against the far right and to unite communities, we should be seeking similar opportunities to establish grassroots campaigns that can meet our collective needs, and enhance our common anti-racist, antifascist goals. The past is not a blueprint, but it does contain important lessons we can apply today.

entry.summary: Ninety years ago this Sunday, antifascist demonstrators routed Oswald Mosley and his supporters when they tried to terrorize the Jews of London’s East End. It’s an important anniversary in a year when a new far-right movement is gathering strength.

entry.title: The Stakes Are High in Brazil’s Upcoming Election

div.p: For a time this summer, Brazil’s presidential election seemed Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s to lose, and Latin America’s largest democracy appeared poised to hold its ground while right-wing candidates triumphed in Colombia, Peru, Honduras, Chile, and Panama, and the Left lost its long hold on Bolivia.

Before, the race had been steadily tightening between the eighty-year-old president and his forty-five-year-old challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, the blandly affable, lacquered version of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a twenty-seven-year sentence for plotting a coup after his defeat. Even before Flávio’s candidacy was announced, polls had put Lula and Jair neck and neck in a hypothetical runoff, though the elder Bolsonaro was already ankle monitor–bound and barred from candidacy.

But Lula’s campaign was jolted back to life in July 2025, when President Donald Trump, following lobbying by Flávio’s brother, Eduardo, intervened on behalf of the embattled former president. Eduardo — a Texas-based, Steve Bannon–linked convicted criminal — urged American pressure in the name of Brazil’s “political prisoners,” and soon Trump announced 50 percent tariffs on Brazilian imports, followed by financial sanctions on Alexandre de Moraes, the supreme court justice overseeing Bolsonaro’s trial.

Lula’s government seized on the affront and made quick work of Trump’s political gift. Within a day of the tariff announcement, it had released an advertisement chiding the gringos for spelling Brasil with a Z; here, the narrator explained, it was spelled with an “S” — for sovereignty. Social media was plastered with images of colossal American flags unfurled at Bolsonaro rallies. And, in a televised address to the nation, Lula declared, “Brazil has only one owner — the Brazilian people.” His message was forceful and unabashedly nationalist, while the Bolsonaro family’s appeals to Washington made its own professions of national pride look pathetically conditional.

The strategy seemed to have worked, at least temporarily. By August 2025, a Quaest poll put Lula 12 points ahead of Bolsonaro in a hypothetical runoff. Then, the following May, Flávio’s death knell seemed to sound when The Intercept revealed that he had solicited $24 million from Daniel Vorcaro, the disgraced Banco Master owner jailed on suspicion of multibillion-dollar fraud. In a turn almost too obliging to be true, it was revealed that the massive sum was solicited to fund Dark Horse, a lavish, soapy propaganda film about Flávio’s father’s rise and survival of an assassination attempt starring Jim Caviezel, who played Jesus in Mel Gibson’s The Passion of the Christ.

Flávio had publicly denied having personal contact with the banker. Yet the day before Vorcaro was arrested while preparing to board a private jet bound for Malta, Flávio had sent the banker a WhatsApp message reading, “Brother, I am and always will be with you.”

In a country particularly sensitive to political corruption scandals, and with voters uninspired by either candidate, the morass seemed close to the worst thing that could have happened to Flávio. In Datafolha’s next survey, Lula broke once more from tied runoff projections, gaining a 4-point advantage.

But the political blaze soon spread toward Lula. On September 1, newly disclosed messages recovered by federal police showed Vorcaro seeking advice and intervention from Justice Alexandre de Moraes, even asking whether he should leave the country. Moraes’s replies were not recovered, and he denied acting on the banker’s behalf, but file metadata also indicated that a draft of his wife’s firm’s whopping R$131 million contract with Banco Master had been edited under a user profile bearing the justice’s name.

Though the Banco Master scandal implicates Flávio and not Lula, it has become particularly damaging for the latter because Lula is seen as a key ally of Moraes. The jurist has attracted controversy for his role in overseeing Bolsonaro’s prosecution and helping annul the ginned-up charges that led to Lula’s imprisonment until 2019. The most recent polls once again show Lula and Flávio at a stalemate, leaving observers of Brazilian politics waiting either for another sordid revelation, or the very likely possibility of another bumbling intervention from Washington.

Lula’s campaign has already had to contend with a right-dominated media at home and interference from abroad. Most recently, Meta inexplicably blocked his campaign social media account for a period less than two weeks before the election, then lifted the ban. This past week, intelligence officials in Brasilia have briefed French and German officials on possible American and Russian attempts to influence the elections.

But the preoccupation with scandal that has defined coverage of the election also obscures a more stubborn problem for the incumbent. He has a substantial record to defend, and yet considerable difficulty persuading Brazilians that his leadership made their lives better.

Brazil’s economy has fared anomalously well by regional standards. Unemployment stood at just 5.3 percent in the quarter through August, and between 2023 and 2024, 8.6 million people were lifted out of poverty. Lula restored increases in the minimum wage above inflation, expanded payments to families with young children, and secured a significant tax exemption for low-income people. He has continued the tangible improvements that made him the most popular president in Brazilian history during his second term.

Yet slowing inflation has not undone years of rising prices, while expensive credit eats into what savings families have. By June, debt repayments excluding mortgages absorbed more than a quarter of aggregate household income. Meanwhile, the war with Iran has put renewed pressure on prices.

Lula has not been able to satisfy his constituents in part because he is caught representing the interests of two distinct groups. To the cautious financiers and industry leaders that help decide Brazil’s elections, he must be a solidly establishment figure — the levelheaded custodian of an economy whose debts must be paid. To the workers that fueled his political rise and are fed up with the stasis and complacency of a power-mongering, wealth-hoarding few, he must offer clear material support and evidence that things will change. And though the Economist, following much of the anglophone press, has described him as a “doddering leftie” trying to best a “vengeful nepo-baby,” much of the Brazilian left has found Lula altogether too accommodating to the institutions that have failed them As early as 2010, early leaders on the left wing of Lula’s Workers Party (PT) began lamenting that, in the words of Plínio de Arruda Sampaio, “The leadership abandoned the PT’s project and embraced the pursuit of power.” The metalworker who lost a finger on the job and forged his political reputation rousing crowds of union workers in the late 1970s is now having difficulty convincing voters that he hasn’t grown too comfortable with the establishment he once promised to challenge.

Nonetheless, Flávio’s stubborn buoyancy in the race should be cause for alarm well beyond the Left. For all his air of managerial sobriety, the dutiful heir could prove far more destructive to Brazilian democracy than his father.

During his presidency, Jair Bolsonaro threatened to disobey judicial rulings, defamed the country’s voting system, and promoted military officials who were later convicted alongside him for a coup conspiracy that included plans to assassinate Lula. But when he entered office in 2019, his authoritarian ambitions were constrained by solid institutions built to withstand attempts to erode democracy. Principally, he was checked by an unusually powerful supreme court, armed with sweeping constitutional and criminal jurisdiction under the 1988 Constitution that was adopted after decades of military dictatorship.
But much has changed since 2019, and those restraints can no longer be taken for granted. Nor can the survival of the democracy they helped preserve.

To begin with, regardless of the presidential outcome, the Chamber of Deputies is expected to remain dominated by the center and Right, while the Right could substantially strengthen its position in the Senate. There, Flávio has explicitly campaigned to build a Bolsonarista coalition willing to impeach Moraes and other supreme court justices. Even without an impeachment majority, a victorious Flávio could gut the court. Two of its eleven justices were appointed by his father, three reach compulsory retirement age by the end of 2030, and one seat remains vacant. If that vacancy survives Lula’s term, Flávio could appoint four justices — with Senate approval — bringing the number chosen by the family to six, a majority.

For a court that has ordered a sitting congressman’s arrest, blocked social media accounts, and suspended X throughout the country, and that has the power to do much else, such capture would give Flávio the power to govern with impunity. With control of the courts and congress, “democratic backsliding” is about the best outcome one could hope for.

Freedom of speech and of dissent would be eroded. Jair routinely smeared and discredited journalists, even weaponizing dictatorship-era censorship laws. Alongside the building of five El Salvador–style megaprisons, Flávio has proposed barring parts of school curricula that conflict with parents’ religious or moral beliefs. He has also sought to replace racial quotas in public-service recruitment with income-based preferences and, in a 2011 interview, called the sight of two men kissing “disgusting.”

Abroad, Flávio’s flimsy nationalism would likely give way to vassalage to Washington. In June, he wrote to Marco Rubio offering to place his prospective transition team “immediately at your disposal” to negotiate a trade and investment agreement. But following Washington into confrontation with Beijing could prove expensive for Brazil. China has eclipsed the United States as a more reliable market for Brazilian exports, buying nearly 29 percent in 2025 against America’s 11 percent, and Chinese companies invested another $6.1 billion into Brazilian infrastructure that year.

The most lasting and globally reaching damage, however, would be environmental. Flávio has dismissed human-caused global warming and mocked the idea that forests generate rainfall, even though reduced rainfall is already harming Brazilian soybean yields. He has coauthored a bill to open mandatory vegetation reserves on rural properties to clearing and backed proposals restricting indigenous claims to ancestral land, alongside expanding oil and gas infrastructure and legalizing fracking.

If his father’s presidency offers anything like a preview, the consequences will be disastrous. Jair hobbled environmental enforcement, making illegal clearing easier and punishment less likely. As a result, annual deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon surged by 54 percent between 2018 and 2022, reaching a fifteen-year high in 2021. Further destruction could help push the forest beyond recovery. A study published in Nature this May found that warming of 1.5–1.9°C above preindustrial levels, combined with the clearing of roughly a quarter of the Amazon — which stores carbon equivalent to roughly fifteen to twenty years of global emissions — could trigger widespread ecological collapse. No subsequent government can simply replace vanished rainforest or recapture lost carbon.

Yet a Bolsonaro restoration is by no means assured. The coalition that returned Lula to office — organized labor, the rural and urban poor, and progressive sections of the middle class — has frayed but retains considerable strength. Its roots run especially deep in the northeast, where Lula’s Bolsa Família program has long supplemented the meager incomes of working families. It remains to be seen, however, whether right-leaning women will see through Flávio’s shallow attempts to win their votes by mentioning his mother, in an attempt to erase the caustically sexist — and eminently unpopular — legacy of his father from their minds. Nor is it clear that the next Vorcaro WhatsApp screenshot will matter more to voters than the price of groceries or the prospect of getting home safely.

At the height of the dictatorship, as military police tortured and jailed dissidents, Chico Buarque released “Apesar de Você,” a somber but resolute samba. To slide the track past state censors, it clothed a resonant challenge to the regime in a quarrel between lovers. “Despite you,” he sang, “tomorrow will be another day.” The censors eventually caught on and banned it. But by then, a hundred thousand copies had sold.
