entry.title: West Point’s Honor Code Taught the Military to Lie

div.p: On May 12, 1962, General Douglas MacArthur strode into the West Point mess hall and delivered a stirring farewell address before an audience of more than two thousand cadets. It had been just over a year since another famed former general, President Dwight D. Eisenhower, had famously delivered his own closing warning about industry’s capture of the Pentagon. Now MacArthur seemed worried about the corruption of the American soldier’s soul — the death of honor itself.

Honor was everything to MacArthur. Between 1919 and 1922, as West Point superintendent, he built cadet life around the academy’s hallowed motto, “Duty, Honor, Country.” He further instituted a cadet honor code and attendant honor boards, a quasi-judicial trial system meant to discourage unethical behavior and promote a culture of leadership among fledgling recruits.

While honor is traditionally equated with honesty, integrity, and accountability, it doesn’t require any of these things by definition. Rather, it denotes fidelity to an institution’s core rites and standards, making it a fragile, fungible concept whose strictures shift depending on who is giving the orders.

In the mess hall that day, MacArthur conjured honor in its purest form, urging the sea of cadets before him “to learn to stand up in the storm, but to have compassion on those who fall; to master yourself before you seek to master others; to have a heart that is clean, a goal that is high.” He called upon them “to be modest so that you will remember the simplicity of true greatness, the open mind of true wisdom, the meekness of true strength.”

MacArthur was a fearsome figure, but like any good military mind, he knew the importance of building soldiers with camaraderie, humility, and intelligence. In his stint as West Point superintendent, MacArthur cut down on hazing and expanded academic freedom. He took the education of these warriors in training seriously, even fortifying the humanities as a critical part of their moral development. For the first time, he provided cadets with access to the daily newspapers, a policy that was viciously opposed by a cadre of influential graduates who prized West Point’s insularity. After just three years on the job, that influential cadre, now ensconced in the War Department, transferred MacArthur to the Philippines and reversed his dictate.

MacArthur’s ideal of the honorable, well-read, and well-rounded officer was an inspiring conception of service but one that would soon come under grave threat from West Point’s superintendent, William Westmoreland, who, a year after MacArthur’s speech, departed the school to run a campaign in Vietnam racked by war crimes, cooked books, and countless strategic failures. During a sojourn to MacArthur’s apartment at the Waldorf Astoria just before this appointment, the wizened general told Westmoreland that the war in southeast Asia was “fraught with hazards” and could only be won with a “scorched earth policy.”

Despite Westmoreland’s profound shortcomings and corruption, he, like many other military architects in Vietnam, would retire in good standing, his reputation helpfully revised via a fawning biography written by West Point’s chair of American history.

As the war corroded both honesty and integrity throughout the ranks, heady notions like honor were reduced to meaningless platitudes. President Richard Nixon frequently invoked the vagaries of honor to mask Vietnam’s discredited premise and the degenerate killing that proliferated. When, on January 23, 1973, Nixon announced the end of the war in a short but defiant speech, he used the phrase “peace with honor” five times.

The same year as Nixon’s speech, Captain Michael Rose, a young Air Force Academy graduate studying at New York University Law School, published A Prayer for Relief, a damning 253-page investigation into the dysfunctions of MacArthur’s beloved Cadet Honor Code.

Over months, Rose collected interviews and intelligence from major training grounds for future military brass, among them all five service academies, including West Point and the Air Force Academy, plus the Virginia Military Institute and the Citadel. His inquiry was powerfully cosigned by a contingent of federal lawmakers, who explicitly counseled military schools to accommodate Rose’s requests for access. They did so begrudgingly, especially at West Point, which actively frustrated his efforts. “The military police there were following me,” he said.

West Point also refused to connect Rose to James Pelosi, a cadet then facing a gauntlet of hazing for failing to immediately put down his pencil at the conclusion of a test. Rose ultimately managed to sneak into West Point’s Camp Buckner, a training facility a few miles from the academy on Lake Popolopen, where he went tent to tent one night looking for Pelosi until he found him. “Then he and I went into the latrine, and I tape-recorded him for an hour.” Pelosi’s assessment of military honor was unsparing. “I’m disillusioned with the air of elitism, of perfection, around here,” he said. “People think that just by being here they’re automatically a little bit better than anyone else. But they’re not.”

Rose’s resulting thesis was simple but devastating: the military’s festering morality crisis — evidenced by “pandemic drug addiction, racial tension, sedition, common crime, refusal of combat duty, widespread assaults and murders of officers [and] rapidly increasing desertion and decreasing reenlistments” — could be traced back to the transactional notions of honor perpetrated at places like West Point.

His argument was crafted from a powerful combination of legalistic analysis and hundreds of vivid interviews from sources sketching out scenes that often seemed plucked from a hard-boiled police drama. Rose documented tainted honor board investigations and corrupt cadet interrogators, some of whom turned off their tape recorders to scream threats at defendants, forcibly cut their hair, and deprive them of sleep. One cadet said the pressure became so bad that he vomited. Others compared the experience to the mock prisoner-of-war interrogation training that school officials had instituted a few months earlier.

Honor-code-related punishments were often biased and freighted with personal baggage. The chairman of one honor board stated his hostility toward a cadet on trial. “This guy has been in trouble before,” he said. “And we don’t want that kind around.” Cadets, many of them under twenty-one, who sought to appeal their honor board decisions were often threatened with a more serious military court-martial, which, due to the military justice system’s punishing and capricious nature, could entail imprisonment at Fort Leavenworth.

Prosecution could stem from any number of offenses. Hundreds of regulations dictating cadet life were itemized in a standard-issue manual known as the Blue Book. Infractions were often vague, making them easily exploitable. They included “general inattention,” “carelessness,” and exercising “poor judgment.” Cadets were technically considered in violation of the honor code for asking a fellow cadet how to spell a word for an essay assignment, or for telling a fib. One cadet who told a superior he had done twenty push-ups when, in fact, he had done eighteen had the book thrown at him. Another who lied about shaving was expelled. Admitting one’s failings could also end in expulsion. “The code,” one West Pointer griped, “weeds out some cadets who are honest enough to report themselves for honor violations.”

Even cadets who reported others for wrongdoing were sometimes expelled for “tolerating” bad behavior, imparting what some administrators quietly worried was a warped lesson, namely that “those who said ‘no comment’ or lied fared better than those who told the truth.” One West Point professor argued that these “seemingly purposeless rules breed resentment,” which in turn curdles into a full-blown rejection of morality. The honor code was a stand-in for respectable behavior, and yet cadets found it nearly impossible to stay in the code’s good graces. It could be fairly reasoned from here that the code was simply too rigid and that rule-breaking was the only way to survive. “Cadets,” Rose’s report concluded, “learn by example that deceit and deception are ‘standard operating procedure’ when the image of West Point or the Army is at stake.” His assertion was backed up by scores of cadets and even in-house psychiatrists. “I hear leaders talking about integrity and spirit and intent,” confessed one cadet. “But I see few who live by their preaching.”

MacArthur’s high-minded crusade a generation earlier had led to something far more brutal and duplicitous than the “Athens on the Hudson” he had prescribed. As one commentator argued in Time magazine, the new batch of senior military leaders tasked with teaching ethics had become infamous for “falsifying body counts, concealing the bombing of Cambodia, [and] covering up My Lai.” At this time, West Point offered a single ethics course, an elective that was only available senior year.

By the Vietnam War’s end, few cadets held MacArthurian feelings about honor. Sixty percent of West Point cadets, for instance, asserted in a 1974 survey that “adherence to the spirit of the Honor Code is deteriorating.” This, according to an accompanying study, could be traced back to the military’s “sanctimonious” belief in honor, which obscured the true knottiness of ethics.

This was a generational loss of military integrity, and yet because it largely played out in academic environments, it often took the form of seemingly insignificant cheating rings. A series of major cheating scandals broke out at the service academies during the Cold War: in 1951, in 1967, in 1972, and then, not long after the fall of Saigon, in 1976. Air Force Academy Dean Robert McDermott defensively blamed the 1967 scandal on civilian counterculture, testifying to congressional investigators that dozens of identified cheaters had hailed from a clique “symbolized by kooky music, long hair, and a few other things.” A subsequent report penned by a committee of retired brass and academics disagreed, blaming the behavior on an academic environment concerned with “the symbols of achievement, sometimes at the expense of reality.”

This shift in military culture was impossibly swift, evident in the case of West Point cadet Joseph Zengerle, whose hopes were high when, as a first-year plebe, he marched at John F. Kennedy’s 1961 inauguration. He absorbed, in person, Kennedy’s rousing call to “ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country.” Months later, he was there in the mess hall for General MacArthur’s humanistic farewell address.

And yet shortly before his graduation from West Point, Zengerle marched at Kennedy’s funeral. The event presaged a darker politics and the continuation of a poisonous war, things that the man in the casket had tried to curb. Soon after, Zengerle was sent to Vietnam to be Westmoreland’s aide-de-camp.
Rose’s report, meanwhile, was ignored, and the Air Force’s judge advocate general declined to certify him as a military lawyer. By the summer of 1974, brass had coerced him to resign.

The deep issues Rose spotlighted continued bubbling up to the surface, often in the form of schoolyard deceptions. In 1976, more than 150 West Point cadets were charged with cheating, this time within the academy’s most storied and prestigious department: electrical engineering. Some assessments later indicated that as many as six hundred cadets had cheated, but even the smaller statistic qualified the 1976 affair as the worst cheating scandal in military history. One of the many cadets forced to resign was Robert K. Koster, son of Samuel Koster, an Army officer who helped cover up My Lai and previously ran West Point.

After the war, many in the Pentagon fell victim to ego, blinkeredness, and historical revisionism. There was no reckoning with the war’s failures. This avoidance was typified by the POW-MIA movement, which, according to historian Rick Perlstein, was used “to justify the carnage in Vietnam in a way that rendered the United States as its sole victim.” Vietnam, along with the civil rights movement, saw the inflammation of the “Lost Cause” myth around the Civil War, manifested when President Nixon attempted to erect a monument to the Confederacy on West Point’s grounds.

Today the warped lessons of the “Lost Cause” and POW-MIA continue to be nurtured by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has himself introduced a new fiction for his generation, namely that DEI was the major cause for America’s losses in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Like MacArthur, Hegseth has made his own rhetorical paeans to honor, writing in his 2024 book The War on Warriors that it was a cornerstone commandment of “America’s civil religion.” By his definition, honor is for those with high casualty counts and reactionary politics. He wrote that honor was under threat from leftist causes, among them: “Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI), Critical Race Theory (CRT), feminism, genderism, safetyism, climate worship, manufactured ‘violent extremism,’ straight-up weirdo shit, and a grab bag of social justice causes.”

Still, in a few fleeting paragraphs, Hegseth offers a cogent analysis of the rot, eloquently fusing MacArthur’s worries about military honesty with Eisenhower’s warnings about military spending. “Once you pin a star on your shoulder, the political pressure mounts,” Hegseth wrote. “Go-along-to-get-along, and get promoted, is the smoothest path. Don’t rock the boat, do what your political masters tell you, never admit mistakes — and get promoted. Then, once you retire, you get to collect a pension and a sweet job from Lockheed Martin.” In these pages, Hegseth proclaims that American generals should be statutorily restricted from comfortably migrating from their “comfy desk jobs in the Pentagon to the boardroom of the military-industrial complex.” It was a veiled swipe, perhaps, at President Joe Biden’s defense secretary, Lloyd Austin, who left a seat on Raytheon’s board to become the first black American to hold the position.

A few months after his book was published, in November 2024, Hegseth was himself unexpectedly nominated to run the Pentagon. During his confirmation hearings, he sketched out how he would construct a hard-charging, unrepentantly violent, and blatantly ahistorical Department of War — departments of mere “defense” were no longer up to the task. In a flash, he dropped any of his past diagnoses about the Pentagon’s true problems, instead hypercharging all the agency’s worst qualities. Hegseth pushed the Pentagon budget past $1 trillion, retaliated against brass simply for their gender or skin color, engaged in war crimes, and prioritized his own future and personal vanity above all else, installing a makeup studio at the Pentagon and having government employees film his workouts and upload them to social media. Hegseth also barred from the Pentagon briefing room photographers who took unflattering photos of him.

At one point during his confirmation hearing, US Senator Elizabeth Warren pressed Hegseth on his shifting stance regarding the dangers of military-industrial influence. “You’re quite sure that every general who serves should not go directly into the defense industry for ten years, but you’re not willing to make that same pledge?” she pressed. Hegseth smirked. “I’m not a general, Senator,” he said.

One of the first things Hegseth did once in office was to crack down on academic freedom at places like West Point, banning books, pushing out professors, and reinterpreting the honor code. In a strange twist, a major ally in his fight is Michael Rose, who, under Biden, became a fierce critic of DEI policies and COVID-19 mandates. In little more than a year, Hegseth has done much damage, though the culture of the US Armed Forces was deeply compromised decades ago. For years, a certain subset of cadets has come to see deception as an ingrained part of military life, represented by a circulating joke about West Point’s motto that goes “Duty, Country, Hon — well, two out of three ain’t bad.”

entry.title: Against the Politics of Communal Fear

div.p: New York City’s new municipal strategy to combat antisemitism comes just days after the war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu used his platform at the United Nations to call Zohran Mamdani “the antisemitic mayor of New York” and claim that since his election “many Jews no longer feel safe” in the city. The initiative seeks to expand education, support victims of hate crimes, and fund security at Jewish institutions and other houses of worship throughout the five boroughs.
Laudable as any attempt to reduce animus is, the Left should view the plan skeptically.

Antisemitism, it goes without saying, is an evil. And it’s an evil that socialists have particular reason to be concerned with. For centuries, the idea that powerful Jewish interests were at the heart of social injustice was widespread. Socialists of August Bebel’s generation called antisemitism “the socialism of fools” for how it steered resentment of capitalist instability and speculation into ethnic hatred.

Today Mamdani is right to condemn it. And it is understandable that he wants to give that condemnation a practical policy expression. This makes sense on the level of both principle and tactics for a political leader who has been the subject of a deliberate and baseless attempt to equate his support for Palestinian freedom with antisemitism.

Any socialist mayor should oppose prejudice, enforce equal rights, and respond to specific acts of discrimination or violence. The question is whether the administration’s response is proportionate to the problem, and whether its rhetoric helps people assess their circumstances accurately or encourages them to understand their lives through a sense of communal siege.

The strategy, produced by the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism, coordinates work across schools, the police, civil rights authorities, and other agencies through an interagency task force. It doubles funding for the broader Partners Against the Hate grants program to $6.4 million and allocates $1 million for security at nonprofits, including synagogues and other houses of worship.

Notably, the report explicitly defends New Yorkers’ right to protest and doesn’t adopt the flawed International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, which has been used to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism. Its commitment to enforcing civil rights and teaching Jewish American history also deserves support. But its account of Jewish insecurity and its outsourcing of much of its work through third-sector organization deserves scrutiny.

Since October 7, 2023, political discourse in New York has been disproportionately concerned with the supposed threats to Jewish New Yorkers, particularly from supporters of Palestinian liberation and Muslim New Yorkers. The campaign against Mamdani intensified that tendency. A secular socialist was portrayed as a Jew-hating Islamist because of his Muslim background and support for Palestinian self-determination. The Israeli government and its supporters, who identify the Jewish people with a violent state, have deliberately blurred the line between being challenged for controversial views (say, defending a genocidal state on a college campus) and being hounded for one’s religious identity.
In reality, NORC research found that people on the hard right held significantly more antisemitic attitudes than other Americans, while those on the hard left held more anti-Israel views.

Still, it’s reasonable to say that amid rising authoritarianism, a right-wing administration, and anger at Israel’s actions, certain forms of antisemitism have grown. These range from naked bigotry to the subtler reification of identity involved in asking Jewish New Yorkers born in the American republic, six thousand miles away, to repent for Israel’s murderous actions.

A real social problem, however, can also acquire the dimensions of a moral panic, and that panic can be weaponized against the Left. Consider a recent example: like other Americans, Asian Americans were victims of violence, some of it racially motivated. Yet the rise of the “Stop Asian Hate” movement brought sweeping claims about what it meant to be Asian in America, rooted in collective vulnerability and identitarian remedies.

Reported hate crimes against Asians did rise during the pandemic amid Donald Trump’s anti-China rhetoric. But the mobilization against those real acts also encouraged a salience bias, in which seemingly every street altercation involving an Asian victim was viewed as a targeted hate crime.

Yet one widely cited tally, from Stop AAPI Hate, consisted mostly of verbal harassment; physical assaults made up about 16 percent of the nearly eleven thousand incidents reported to the organization from March 2020 through December 2021.

Hate crimes against Asians recorded by the NYPD rose sharply, from twenty-eight in 2020 to well over a hundred in 2021. But the movement went further, presenting those attacks as a wave of racist hostility directed at a single community. “Asian American and Pacific Islander” is an umbrella label that groups together people with origins across a vast region, divided by class, language, and national background.

The “Stop Asian Hate” remedies were tautological. The movement insisted there was a mass problem that demanded marches and won corporate declarations against hate, new federal hate crime legislation, and pork for community nonprofits. It didn’t matter that some of the most high-profile incidents fit the story poorly.

In January 2022, Michelle Go was murdered while waiting for a train at Times Square. The man charged with pushing her in front of the train was homeless and had been diagnosed with schizophrenia two decades earlier. A better-staffed public transit system, track barriers, more state funding for psychiatric care, and supportive housing might all have helped prevent Go’s murder. Public education about the contributions of an imagined “AAPI community” would not have.

But organizing around identity made those universal solutions harder, not easier, to imagine. And it taught many Asian Americans to feel irrationally unsafe in the cities and towns where they grew up and to understand their safety in racial terms.

The same dynamics are at play in discussions of antisemitism today. When something happens to a Jewish New Yorker, the first response is seemingly to present the incident as evidence of an all-encompassing danger, making other Jews feel less secure. That fear itself then becomes politically noteworthy: “I don’t feel safe in the city of my birth anymore.” Communal identity becomes even more central to how people understand their lives and their relationships with others.

The statistics often cited in response to arguments like these also deserve scrutiny. Advocacy groups’ incident tallies, police records of hate crimes, and surveys of communal anxiety measure different things. Yet in a climate of fear — whether among Asian Americans a few years ago or Jewish people today — they are conflated into evidence of an emergency.

The Anti-Defamation League’s 2021 audit is instructive. It highlighted a worrying 34 percent increase in antisemitic incidents while acknowledging that many of the incidents were identified through new reporting partnerships. Putting aside well-warranted left-wing skepticism of the ADL, the example shows how changes in data collection can complicate efforts to distinguish changes in underlying behavior from changes in reporting.

Even police data on hate crimes don’t necessarily tell us how likely an Asian American or Jewish New Yorker is to suffer violence. That requires attention to absolute numbers, population, the kinds of offenses involved, and their distribution. It also requires political judgments about whether the response should take the form of universal or identitarian investments, and how those investments should be delivered.

The report’s own rhetoric illustrates some of the confusion. Its opening letters move between assaults, vandalism, and “stares and casual comments” in describing a climate of fear. These experiences require different assessments and responses. Surveys showing widespread anxiety cannot independently establish the prevalence of the conditions people fear. Otherwise, the effects of alarm become its justification.

It doesn’t require ignoring the persistence of antisemitism and the potential for its mass emergence to say that American Jews live in secure, prosperous, and integrated settings. Some heinous speech and sporadic violence should not erase the distance between today’s America and the history of Jewish exclusion.

As Hannah Arendt warned, treating antisemitism as an eternal fact of Jewish life can give antisemites an alibi, making a contingent political prejudice appear natural and inevitable. Ahistorical comparisons trivialize the centuries of subordination, pogroms, and ultimately mass extermination that Jews faced in Europe. Along with anti-American rhetoric like Joe Biden’s absurd claim that without Israel “not a Jew in the world is safe,” such comparisons do a disservice to the long struggle that has made the United States a hospitable home for millions of minorities.

The panics that made some Asians afraid of commuting to work, or some Jewish New Yorkers afraid of their neighbors, also rely on rhetoric that leaves us little room to describe a resurgence of structural discrimination. If there is a real antisemitic political movement growing in this country, beyond the acts of a few depraved people, what anti-Jewish laws is it advancing? How is it organizing to deprive Jews of their rights? What social structures are being built to enforce Jewish exclusion?

Online bigotry from people like Nick Fuentes, or even from some supporters of the Palestinian cause, does not itself demonstrate a mass movement capable of imposing anti-Jewish rule. Nor does it establish how much that bigotry affects Jewish Americans’ daily lives beyond the cycle of panic and the reification of identity it encourages. Cherry-picking speech in a country of more than 340 million people, even when every report is accurate, obscures the broader state of our society.

There is always a danger of accepting our opponents’ misleading accounts of a city rife with hate and communal strife. But Mamdani’s response — that he is the mayor for all New Yorkers — makes both moral and tactical sense. The city’s policy choices, however, deserve scrutiny.

The Left’s answer to communal fear should be a radical assertion of our shared humanity, the same assertion we employ to defend the rights of the starved and maimed people of Palestine. When we encourage an environment where every political discussion has to start with “as a Jew” or “as a Muslim,” we’ve already accepted the idea that our moral obligations have communal boundaries. Among Jewish critics of Israel, the habit is understandable: they are answering a state that falsely claims to speak for Jews everywhere. But no one should have to establish the right ancestry or religion before opposing the killing of Palestinians, just as no one needs to be Jewish to be outraged by a swastika on a synagogue door.

The growth of identitarian rhetoric challenges our broader effort to change New York, a city long shaped by ethnic brokerage through organizations that claim to speak for particular communities. Today that pattern rewards those who can demonstrate not only their group’s political power but also its vulnerability. The spokespeople are, of course, often professionals and capitalists speaking to workers. When city and state governments accept this arrangement, they’re boosting a form of multiculturalism that amounts to: “Hello, Bengali worker, would you feel more comfortable if the city spoke to you via your Bengali slumlord?”

Every new program premised on a communal threat invites other groups’ brokers to make the same case. Socialists should be trying to wind down this system and build organizations on the basis of class identity, not reinforce it in the name of diversity.

This is where Mamdani has been a breath of fresh air. The media constantly talked about his identity and made him address it. But he is most comfortable translating his core universalism into concrete class demands: cheaper rents, free public transit, and universal childcare.

In its delivery mechanisms, however, this new plan to address antisemitism is a (very small) step in the wrong direction. It channels millions through nonprofit organizations for work public agencies could do directly. Some of these organizations are particularly pernicious, like the Jewish Community Relations Council of New York, which explicitly works to build support for Israel and circulates material opposing boycott campaigns against it. No one on the Left should support sending taxpayer funds to such an organization. But even if all the groups were committed solely to hate crime prevention and survivor support, we should ask why public agencies aren’t equipped to meet those needs directly.

This gets to a wider problem. New York responds to social needs by funneling money through nonprofits, often leaving public agencies to administer contracts instead of developing the ability to provide services themselves. Its own investigators have documented conflicts of interest and oversight failures in the nonprofit shelter system. Those failures strengthen the case for a better-funded welfare state that delivers services directly.

A socialist administration should build durable public capacity to address real social problems without reifying either communal identity or the perception of insecurity. In this case, civil rights enforcement and public education campaigns should be carried out entirely by staffed public institutions with transparent budgets and clear performance indicators.

Whatever our assessment of the prevalence of antisemitism in our city, Jewish New Yorkers are entitled to the same freedoms as everyone else, and violations of those freedoms should be addressed. We can uphold those commitments without fueling communalism, by building institutions that improve people’s lives and give them the choice to relate to their identity, or choose not to, in any way that they want.

entry.title: A Decade After His First Presidential Run, Bernie Isn’t Alone

div.p: If you’re anyone who veers remotely to the left politically, there are two eras: a time before Bernie Sanders ran for president, and a time after. The US political landscape before Sanders’s first presidential campaign looks today like an alien planet. There were virtually no socialists who held elected office, or at least those who admitted to it. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) was an obscure organization with a little over six thousand members across twenty-six chapters. Arguably the most prominent leftist figure was a curmudgeonly linguist who almost never appeared in mainstream media, Noam Chomsky. Only 59 percent of Democrats and less than half of independents were willing to vote for a socialist candidate. And the great progressive hope was a politician who flatly opposed single-payer health care and ran on a platform of stronger regulation and more public investment in key industries.

Within five years of Sanders’s run, dozens of open socialists served in elected office at every level of government, including the US Congress. DSA’s membership had exploded to more than 55,000 with more than 150 chapters in every corner of the country. Socialists like Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were among the most popular political figures in the country. The share of Democrats willing to vote for a socialist candidate had jumped to 74 percent. And that progressive politician, Elizabeth Warren, launched a presidential campaign on a platform of single-payer health care, universal childcare, free public college, and debt cancellation.

Neither Sanders nor his campaign were single-handedly responsible for all this. But it’s not a coincidence that the political landscape transformed this drastically, in this particular way, within less than a decade of his first campaign, nor that 97 percent of DSA’s now 120,000-strong membership joined after 2016 (the majority of its current members joined after 2019, when Sanders launched his second run and a year after Ocasio-Cortez first won election). Before Sanders made his first official announcement — to a small crowd of Capitol Hill reporters, muttering that there wasn’t an “endless amount of time” because he’d have to get back to work — most people, even on the Left, would have told you the world we currently inhabit, with all its horrors but also its sudden possibility, was decades away at best.

There were a few socialists in political office before Sanders ran. Kshama Sawant had won a seat on the Seattle city council in 2013, for instance, while Carlos Ramirez-Rosa was sworn into his Chicago alderman’s seat twenty-nine days before Sanders’s announcement, even if he had not run as a socialist. (Ramirez-Rosa joined DSA a few months after Donald Trump won the 2016 election.) But the broad national appeal of Sanders’s platform was something different. It reminded millions of Americans who had learned to instinctively narrow their political ambitions that the things they assumed were impossible — not because they were actually impractical, but because there seemingly wasn’t the political will — they could and should fight for, because it was what most people wanted.

Sanders’s campaign showed it was possible for a socialist to win over people who had never even flirted with New Deal liberalism, let alone Marxism. Whatever drove it, whether Sanders’ authenticity, his fist-shaking against the establishment, or the fact that even conservative households don’t want to be buried alive in medical bills, Sanders had a crossover appeal that defied the way we tend to pigeonhole voters. It wasn’t out of the ordinary to hear Trump supporters in those years professing that, after the demagogic billionaire, Bernie was their guy.

Ideas and policies were one thing, but Sanders gave today’s socialists a ready-made vocabulary and approach to sell them, too. The Left’s decades in the political wilderness had been an often fruitless, Goldilocks-style search for a political tribune. Before Sanders, the lefty firebrands who championed the causes he became famous for came off, however unfairly, as kooks — like Dennis Kucinich, whose penchant for ventriloquism and claims he had seen a UFO could overshadow his advocacy for single-payer health care, or Mike Gravel, whose antiwar message was undercut by an onstage style that came off as unhinged ranting. Lefty politicians either had vision but not credibility, or, in Warren’s case, credibility but without a sufficiently ambitious vision.

Sanders, by contrast, came off as fairly normal but serious — neither an ideological zealot, nor a doctrinaire leftist who spoke in slogans or obscure jargon, but someone who put socialist ideas into everyday language and made you agree they were common sense. What eccentricities he had built up in the course of a lifetime were either helpful — the uncombed hair, rumpled suits, and distaste for chit-chat that so amused political reporters bolstered his image as a no-nonsense fighter — or ones he swiftly repudiated.

As Americans watched and heard Sanders speak with their own eyes and ears, they didn’t see the caricature of a socialist they had been fed through popular culture, but a pissed-off fighter for the working Americans being perennially screwed by a host of nefarious forces they recognized in their own lives: big banks, health insurers, corrupt politicians, the billionaires that fund them. This had been the secret sauce of Sanders’s breakthrough election to the US Congress in 1990, when he had used the previous year’s savings and loan bailout as a political foil and saw passing motorists yell at him to “Give ’em hell, Bernie!”

They also saw someone who rooted this pitch in a national tradition they understood. Yes, Sanders often pointed to European countries like Denmark and Sweden to show that the policies he was calling for were practical. But crucially, he wrapped himself in the coat of the New Deal, the most well-known historical parallel to what he envisioned for the country, eschewing the tendency of some radicals to dismiss Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s program as a series of mere liberal reforms that had done capitalism a favor.

In his first run, just as he would in his second, Sanders delivered a major address explaining to the nation what democratic socialism meant by casting the national memory back to the New Deal. Sanders had good reason to do it beyond its historical legibility for American voters. After all, for all its compromises, the greatest, longest-lasting achievements of Roosevelt’s program were often demanded, drawn up, and put into motion by left-wing radicals.

It took a little longer for the class of young socialists inspired by Sanders to absorb all of these lessons. Many clung to the judgmental moralism and jargon-littered vocabulary that became accepted as normal on the Left for far too long. And socialists’ self-defeating fixation on “abolition” of police and prisons still persists, in spite of its many political and practical downsides.

But they have been absorbed. We see it in the more plainspoken communication style and more class-focused approach of Ocasio-Cortez, who these days tends to stress the power of billionaires instead of simply racism to explain the Right’s ascent, and who is more likely to talk about how “the American Revolution was against the billionaires of their time” than to talk about “the intersectionality of interconnectedness of all our fights” for a laundry list of types of justice.

And we see it in the mayoralty of Zohran Mamdani, one the most popular politicians in the country, who has charted a different path on public safety and policing that more closely parallels that of Sanders, whose very first election victory rested on poaching the local police union’s endorsement.

All of the elements that built and sustained Sanders’s political path through an era vastly more unfriendly to socialism were there in his first campaign. That campaign in turn became a real-world model for socialists in the twenty-first century to both run for office and engage with a skeptical American public — a model that, looking out from the cliffside of 2026, they have used to reshape US politics.

Trump’s two election victories and the weakness of liberal institutions have made it easy to miss this story. It’s been made even easier thanks to a mainstream press perpetually in a hurry to declare the Left dead, confidently telling us over and over again that the socialist movement Sanders’s run helped breathe new life into had finally run out of oxygen.

The reality is that a decade after a time when, generously, only a handful of socialists around the country held any elected office, socialists now hold serious positions of power all over. There will be at least seven socialists in the US House of Representatives next year, growing nearly fourfold since Trump declared to a standing ovation from Congress that “America will never be a socialist country.”

A socialist will almost certainly be elected mayor of the nation’s capital this November. Socialists are presidents of the city councils of both St Louis, Missouri, and Providence, Rhode Island, with the candidate’s slate of progressive allies achieving a near sweep of their city council races in the latter. Socialists also control a third of Portland, Oregon’s city council, occupy nearly a third of the seats on Minneapolis’s — where DSA-backed members serve as both the majority and minority leaders — and have four seats on Los Angeles’s fifteen-member city council. Wisconsin has a socialist caucus again in its state legislature after a nearly hundred-year absence, one of whose members very nearly took the Democratic nomination for governor this year. For years, socialists held a near-majority on the city council of Somerville, Massachusetts.

Numbering in the dozens at the end of last decade, there are now more than 250 socialists holding elected office across the country. You can find them everywhere from the Mountain States (in Santa Fe, Missoula, Aurora, to name a few) and the Midwest (in Toledo, Louisville, Iowa, Chicago, among others) to New England (in places like Portland, Cambridge, the state legislatures of Vermont and Connecticut), and the South (in New Orleans, Atlanta, Knoxville, San Antonio, and more).

And of course, in New York, a socialist governs the country’s biggest city, the home of its financial sector and the largest city economy in the world, helped by four fellow socialists on its city council and a total of sixteen who will sit in the state legislature after November. Long before this, with much smaller numbers, socialists in the state, including Mamdani himself, had already played leading roles in major progressive legislative victories, passing sweeping eviction protections and allowing the state’s largest public utility to enter the renewable energy industry, among other things.

Many of these officials were directly inspired by Sanders. Ocasio-Cortez, Rep. Summer Lee, former fellow Squad member Cori Bush, and Massachusetts state representative Erika Uyterhoeven all volunteered or worked on his 2016 run. Mamdani has pointed squarely at that campaign as the reason he became a socialist. Other socialist mayors-to-be, like Providence’s David Morales and Washington, DC’s Janeese Lewis George, have credited it with their political awakening. So have socialist Squad-member-in-waiting Claire Valdez and St Petersburg city council member Richie Floyd, the first socialist elected in Florida in a hundred years. Go to any moderately large gathering of socialists, whether elected officials, rank-and-file DSAers, or both, and you’re likely to see “Bernie 2016” memorabilia sprinkled throughout.

Attached again to concrete policies and living, flesh-and-blood political figures, socialism is not the boogeyman it used to be. Most Democratic voters, a third of whom now identify as democratic socialists, are perfectly happy to have a socialist as their candidate, or even actively prefer a candidate endorsed by one. Multiple polls show voters across the board are more turned off by MAGA candidates and Trump endorsees than self-described democratic socialists. In both pure numbers and political power, the current crop of socialist elected officials may be far away from the movement’s American zenith in the early twentieth century, but none of this suggests they’re anywhere close to hitting their ceiling yet.

The question is whether they and the movement around them can sustain this upward trajectory. In some ways, Sanders’s path to the presidential race, spread out over thirty-five years in which socialists wandered the desert, was easier than the one his political heirs now have to traverse. Not only is state repression of the Left ramping up to levels far beyond where it was even under Ronald Reagan, but high-profile socialists are today as likely to face attacks and misinformation coming from pockets of the Left as from the Right.

Sanders too spent his career being pelted by many of the same left-wing accusations his 2020s successors now face: that he was a traitor to the cause, an imperialist, a liberal, a fraud, too accommodationist to the Democratic Party, and so on. Lobbed at a time when the Left was small and marginal, none of it stuck by the time Sanders ran in 2015, when he was viewed in the fresh eyes of both friend and foe as a uniquely, even naively, principled and pure idealist — instead of the shrewd, ruthlessly pragmatic operator he actually was.

It was just as well. An unyielding pragmatic radicalism has always been at the heart of Sanders’s approach. As he followed its glow, millions of others trailed after its familiar incandescence. And when the light grew just bright enough, he turned around and saw something remarkable: that he was no longer alone.

entry.title: Jordan Bardella Isn’t Such a Friend of Jews After All

div.p: As a young member of the Front National (today’s Rassemblement National), Jordan Bardella was an “obsessive antisemite,” according to a story published by investigative site Mediapart this Monday. “Banks are all controlled by Jews,” Bardella allegedly wrote in one message published by Mediapart. “The Jew must dominate other peoples, crush them and rob them,” read another. “A Zionist is necessarily Jewish, and deeply so.”

Bardella, who was the Rassemblement National’s candidate for prime minister in 2024 and who has been president of the party since 2022, denies having written the messages, which Mediapart says date from between 2013 and 2015.

“These comments are completely outrageous. They’re not mine. . . . I dispute them,” Bardella said in a television interview on Monday night, adding that his lawyers had filed a defamation lawsuit against Mediapart. “I think we’re looking at something very organized . . . which resembles a covert operation.”
Bardella also claimed that the messages that he says he didn’t write, when he was around seventeen years old, weren’t from a time when he had any sort of leadership position in the party.
Bardella joined Jean-Marie Le Pen’s Front National when he was sixteen, then became head of the Seine-Saint-Denis branch of the party in 2014, when he was nineteen.

During his rise as the fresh young face of the far-right party, Bardella was feted in the media as a representative of a new version of the Front National that had shed its roots in the fascist underworld to become a party like any other, free from its racist heritage.

“They present a young, cosmopolitan . . . image for the Front National,” the news channel BFMTV wrote in 2016 about a group of party activists from France’s suburbs. “Their figurehead: Jordan Bardella, regional councilor for Île-de-France [the region around Paris] at just twenty-one.”

At about the same time, according to Mediapart, Bardella was swimming in a soup of late 2000s and early 2010s French “new right” ideology, which has close affiliations with fascism and classic French antisemitism.

Its chief ideologue, Alain Soral, became a viral celebrity online for his syncretic analysis of French society, which wed racist, anti-immigrant ideology to a type of motley anti-Zionism based fundamentally in antisemitism, with a few anti-imperialist geopolitical positions soldered on. In the late 2000s, Soral was close with and wrote speeches for Jean-Marie Le Pen, still the party’s leader then. Soral became a member of the Front National’s central committee but left in 2009 when he was denied leadership of the party’s list for the European elections.

“His analyses are correct because everything is verified by the facts,” Bardella wrote of Soral in 2013, per Mediapart. “Zionism and domination by the banks are linked (Goldman Sachs, Rothschild, Lehman Brothers. . . . ).”
“I knew Bardella a little; I had some conversations with him,” Soral said in 2025. “On certain radical subjects, he wasn’t as innocent as he seems.”
“Jordan watched kilometers of Soral videos and read his books,” a former “close adviser” to Bardella told Mediapart. “He became politicized partially because of it.”

Marine Le Pen, the party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, expelled her father from the Front National in 2015 after he refused to apologize for calling the gas chambers in the Holocaust a “detail” of history that didn’t matter much then defended Marshal Philippe Pétain, the general who collaborated with the Nazis during the World War II–era occupation of France.

Jean-Marie Le Pen’s expulsion was supposed to represent the culmination of this strategy of “dédiabolisation” — literally “de-demonization.” The National Rally may have been founded by at least one former member of the Waffen-SS, the message was, but Le Pen père’s expulsion was the end result of a cleanup operation by Le Pen fille to push out the embarrassing remnants who were still partial to a Roman salute every once in a while (“I’ll never forgive my decision [to expel my father], because I know that it caused him an immense amount of pain,” Le Pen said in 2025).

In the 2010s, Louis Aliot theorized that shedding the Front National’s antisemitic image was one of the last barriers it had to surmount to become electable. Aliot visited Israel — a first for a politician from his party — and actively cultivated links with Israel’s political class.

Aliot, who once lived with Marine Le Pen and still has an excellent relationship with her family, is today vice president of the Rassemblement National as well as mayor of Perpignan. He continues to play an influential role in the party, which has wholeheartedly adopted the strategy of pushing Zionism as a defense against historical charges of antisemitism.

Marine Le Pen has called the party the “shield” of Jews in France against radical Islam, painting France’s Arab and Muslim population as a threat to Jews, an echo of familiar neoconservative narratives of a “clash of civilizations.”

As president of the party, Bardella has kept the ship steady and continued to present the Rassemblement National as French Jews’ best ally, mostly through ostentatious pro-Zionist posturing. In 2025, Bardella visited Jerusalem as an official representative for the party at an Israeli government-sponsored conference on fighting antisemitism.
That’s the angle that the party, which fallen into formation to claim Mediapart’s story is a hoax, is taking to defend Bardella.

“I saw him at Yad Vashem, at the Nova site, in the kibbutz of Netiv HaAsara slain on October 7 . . . then in Jerusalem to bring the voice of our party into the fight against antisemitism,” a parliamentary assistant for the Rassemblement National in the EU Parliament posted. “The controversies will pass. What I saw and heard there nobody can take away.”

“Mediapart is a far-left newspaper,” the party’s vice president, Aliot, told me on Tuesday, after I asked if the Rassemblement National believed the accusations against Bardella were true. “No comment.”

Mediapart responded by saying that if its credibility continued to be questioned, it would be releasing the documents that it based its reporting on. Erik Tegnér, the founder of a far-right media organization called Frontières, posted that Bardella was essentially the target of right-wing elected officials who regularly leaked to Mediapart, amid speculation that the story could have been planted by Le Pen and her allies to push Bardella out of the party after tensions following her decision to run for president.
Meanwhile, it’s egg on the face for France’s liberals and centrists who’ve made a big show about the party’s evolution into becoming a responsible party of government.

Serge Klarsfeld, a French historian and lawyer who spent his career chasing Nazi war criminals and documenting France’s role in deporting Jews during the Holocaust, drew condemnation from many when he met with Marine Le Pen in 2024, then said he would vote “without hesitation” for the Rassemblement National over the left-wing France Insoumise.
“The RN supports Jews, supports the state of Israel. It’s normal that between an antisemitic party and a pro-Jewish party, I’d vote for the pro-Jewish party,” Klarsfeld said.
False critiques of Jean-Luc Mélenchon and France Insoumise have multiplied since October 2023 because of the party’s support for Palestine and condemnation of Israel’s genocide.

A frequent accusation against France Insoumise these days is that it, and not the Rassemblement National, is today the party of antisemitism in France. This attitude is said to be fueled by a desire for votes from young Arab, African, and Muslim voters in the poor suburbs who are susceptible to a Soralite blend of anti-Zionism. That’s despite France Insoumise’s clear rejection of antisemitism and the doubtful prospect that this caricatured electorate actually exists.
Meanwhile, the Rassemblement National coasts on a reputation promoted endlessly by figures in the media and the government that it has changed and is no longer a racist or antisemitic force.

“The Rassemblement National belongs to the republican arc,” Bruno Retailleau — who was Emmanuel Macron’s interior minister across multiple governments, and is president of the mainstream conservative party Les Républicains — said last summer, using a phrase that means a party is within the realm of legitimate political expression in France.

Retailleau, a particularly noxious anti-immigrant French nationalist, may offer better proof that France’s conservatives have radicalized than that anything fundamental has changed about the Rassemblement National.

“Politics is communication,” Bardella reportedly wrote in the messages over a decade ago. “Ever since [Marine Le Pen’s] speech got cleaned up the number of voters has exploded,” he explained, while celebrating that the party “has stayed true to its founding ideology” for “more than 40 years.” He might insist otherwise today, but I think he was on to something.

entry.title: American Capitalism Isn’t Just Billionaires

div.p: When one thinks of the rich in the United States, the first people who come to mind are the megabillionaires whose extravagant consumption, eye-popping wealth, and notorious political interventions have transformed them into household names. Perched atop the Forbes 400 list of America’s richest individuals are Silicon Valley moguls and Wall Street executives who command some of the most prominent corporations in America.

Beneath this elite stratum of capitalists lies a vastly less conspicuous group of still-wealthy but lesser-known business owners. Far more numerous and more geographically dispersed across the country than their billionaire brethren, this “American Gentry” exercises great influence on local, state, and even national politics. The relatively scant attention they receive compared to their headline-grabbing compatriots means that their collective effect on the American wealth distribution has been hitherto mostly unexamined.

A new book by Princeton economist Owen Zidar and University of Chicago economist Eric Zwick attempts to correct this relative neglect by quantifying the place of “The Everywhere Millionaire” in the American wealth distribution. The book is a popular exposition of previous academic work that celebrated scholars of inequality Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman deemed (despite some critiques) an “important contribution” to the estimation of wealth inequality in the United States.

What emerges from Zidar and Zwick’s investigations is the fundamental role of “pass-through” businesses in securing their owners a place near the top of the American wealth distribution. Changes to the tax code in the past half century, some lobbied for by the very business owners receiving their benefits, have made the pass-through business structure even more profitable than it would have been otherwise. The result is an astounding amount of wealth collected by the American Gentry, who often employ it toward corrosive, self-serving political ends.

header.h2: Do Not Pass Through, Do Not Collect $200

div.p: Zidar and Zwick coin the term “Main Street Millionaires” (MSMs) to signify households with at least $5 million in wealth (meaning they are in the top 4 percent of the US wealth distribution) and private business ownership. This group, around three million in number, collectively owns an impressive thirteen times the combined wealth of the Forbes 400.

The collective wealth of the MSMs has more than doubled over the course of the twenty-first century, to the point where it presently stands at around $55 trillion. MSMs are also more geographically dispersed than their Forbes 400 colleagues. Half of the latter live in New York City, San Francisco, Los Angeles, or Miami, whereas less than a quarter of the MSMs do.

The businesses that MSMs run are often classified as pass-through entities in the tax code, which include sole proprietorships, partnerships, limited liability companies, and S corporations. Unlike a C corporation, which treats the company as a separate taxpaying entity from its owners, pass-throughs do not pay corporate or dividend taxes, and instead their profits pass through to the owners’ individual income taxes.

The Tax Reform Act of 1986, which pushed the top individual tax rate below the corporate tax rate for several years, triggered a major shift in the legal structure of American business. The result is that today 95 percent of all US businesses are pass-throughs, accounting for the employment of half of all American workers and more than half of American business income. Indeed, Zidar and Zwick and other coauthors have calculated that 41 percent of the rise in the income share of the top 1 percent of Americans since 1980 is due to pass-through income.

With almost all US businesses now classified as pass-throughs of one sort or another, the businesses the MSMs own run the gamut of American commerce. Zidar and Zwick profile businesses that manufacture everything from seamless gutters to tanning beds to laboratory chemicals to quiche and provide services that span from ambulance billing to trade show planning. It should be stressed, however, that private business is not necessarily small business. Major corporations such as Fidelity and Hobby Lobby are registered as pass-throughs, while large firms like Koch and Mars are private C corporations. But even more modest MSMs can generate serious profits, as the authors demonstrate with some revealing figures. For instance, “there are 25 autodealers [in the top 0.1 percent of the US income distribution] for every member of the Forbes 400.”

Previous attempts to more comprehensively map the upper reaches of the wealth distribution used one of three methodologies, all of which generated results but had various shortcomings: surveys, investigative reporting, and nonlinked databases. Surveys have limited coverage, face difficulty cajoling the rich to disclose information about their financial situation, and are sometimes subject to anonymization procedures precisely to prevent users from linking the data to identifiable persons. Investigative reporting’s reach is inherently limited; even the people behind cataloging the Forbes 400 can’t be certain that they are not overlooking less ostentatious billionaires. Finally, nonlinked databases are not as useful as those that can match their data to others.

Zidar and Zwick instead follow the lead of Thomas Piketty and his collaborators in using tax data as their fundamental data source. The core methodological innovation informing the book’s findings is the linkage of tax databases within the US Department of the Treasury to match businesses to their owners and employees (all anonymized). The authors then combed through auxiliary sources, such as registries of private jet and yacht owners, to attempt to deanonymize these millionaires. Resulting interviews with various capitalists the authors identified comprise a significant portion of the book.

Zidar and Zwick frame their findings as a contrarian exercise highlighting how much relatively unassuming professions contribute to the upper layers of the American wealth distribution. However, some of the evidence they present in the book qualifies this narrative. A table showing the industries generating the most pass-through income is heavily populated by the highly paid professions one might expect: lawyers, doctors, financiers, accountants, dentists, realtors, architects, and consultants. To be sure, plenty of more plebeian businesses are represented as well: lumberyards, motorcycle dealers, and paper product distributors, for instance, and these less glamorous trades are often the focus of the book’s anecdotes.

Part of the story of the MSMs’ affluence is the squeezing of their workers. Smaller businesses are legally exempt from many of the labor protections that larger corporations must enforce. For instance, the Family and Medical Leave Act only applies to firms with fifty or more employees, portions of the Civil Rights Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act only fully apply at a fifteen-employee threshold, the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act only regulates employers with at least one hundred workers, and the Affordable Care Act’s requirement that businesses provide their employees health insurance only kicks in at a minimum of fifty employees. On top of these difficulties, smaller shops are notoriously harder to unionize.

Zidar and Zwick briefly weigh in on the controversy regarding why labor faces an ongoing decline in its share of national income. One factor they highlight as driving this trend is the increasing use of noncompete agreements to discourage workers — now even low-paid and entry-level ones — from switching employers. In previous work, Zidar and Zwick and coauthors suggested that a third of the declining labor share was a statistical artifact created by the classification of many American businesses as pass-through entities.

When assessing the effect of MSMs on politics, it’s noteworthy that MSMs themselves make up a significant share of American politicians. Nearly a quarter of congressional representatives own a business, as do over 40 percent of legislators at the state level and a third of all mayoral candidates. This means that a large share of legislators have a personal incentive to support the interests of business owners generally and individually will be tempted to promote their own business interests.

MSMs have secured anticompetitive legal protection of their businesses in a variety of industries, pushing up costs for consumers. Beer distributors, for example, benefit from laws that prevent brewers from also owning distribution and make it difficult to terminate a distribution contract. Franchise laws give auto dealers similar protection from rivals. Realtors guarantee their positions as middlemen by restricting access to information about real estate sales. Doctors inflate their profits through restricting access to medical care, which they do by putting a ceiling on the number of residency positions and limiting the ability of nonphysicians to deliver care. Powerful sectional lobbies ensure the maintenance of their members’ privileges through organizations like the National Association of Realtors, American Medical Association, and National Automobile Dealers Association.

MSMs skew politically conservative, and some of them have unsurprisingly used their fortunes to advance right-wing causes. In 2022, the largest federal campaign donors for Republicans were Dick and Liz Uihlein, whose income derives from the shipping supplies company Uline. The late Republican senator and presidential nominee John McCain’s political career was largely funded by his wife’s inherited riches from a beer distribution company.

The MSMs’ political influence has been most nefarious, perhaps, in the domain of taxes. The Internal Revenue Service estimates that around $600 billion dollars of taxes are owed but not paid every year; pass-through owners are responsible for almost half of this “tax gap.” “More than at any recent time,” Zidar and Zwick write, “the tax code for pass-throughs runs on the honor system, with predictable results.”

And MSMs are progressively seeing more tax loopholes enacted to their benefit. Estate taxes have been whittled down to the point where only 0.1 percent of households face an estate tax of any sort. The 2017 Trump tax cuts allowed pass-through owners to deduct 20 percent of business income from their taxes, and the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act made these temporary provisions permanent.

Even though Zidar and Zwick recognize that upward social mobility is becoming more difficult in the United States, a major theme of the book is that the “American Dream” of upward mobility remains attainable, primarily through private business ownership. The authors plainly have admiration for the MSMs who have achieved entrepreneurial success, and much of the text is content drawn from interviews with MSMs about their achievements. Clearly the authors intended these profiles both as ways to de-anonymize the “stealthy wealthy” and to give their account some narrative color, but the stream of self-reported business heroics of various MSMs becomes tedious.

Despite large chunks of the book reading as inspirational literature for aspiring business owners (the largest of three segments is entitled “How To Get Rich”) or a celebration of the everyman capitalist, Zidar and Zwick recognize the negative effects of MSMs in exacerbating social inequality. They end the book with some policy reform proposals, such as raising the minimum wage and reforming the tax code to harmonize tax rates. Useful steps, of course, but these proposals fall far short of a comprehensive program to rein in the economic and political power of the MSMs.

The main value in Zidar and Zwick’s book, however, is not in its politics but in its empirical research. The authors have gone some distance toward unmasking a stratum of the capitalist class that too often escapes recognition, not to mention criticism. A serious left-wing political project needs to grapple with this overlooked but powerful section of the American elite.

entry.title: Eric Hobsbawm Owed His Success to Mass Culture

div.p: More than the “revolutionary historian” promised by the subtitle, the Eric Hobsbawm chronicled in Emile Chabal’s biography is above all a canny academic entrepreneur. Early in his career, Hobsbawm found a literary agent and converted his lectures for undergraduates into a series of best-selling books. He made valuable contacts with rising-star scholars and publishing houses in continental Europe. He traveled widely: not so much for archival research, which he practiced sparingly, but for conferences, lectures, and intellectual tourism in appealing destinations. The Soviet Union, which occupied a central place in his thought for obvious reasons, did not qualify for more than a brief, unpleasant visit.

He displayed a knack for keeping himself in the public eye, with a steady stream of journalism and polemics, and for a degree of tactical adaptation. In the 1980s, he pivoted from writing the histories of the working class that defined his early work to studies of nationalism and invented traditions. By the late 1990s, he had achieved such eminence that he could turn down a knighthood while requesting — and receiving — a considerably more prestigious and exclusive appointment to the Order of the Companions of Honour, an award also tied to the monarchy but with less symbolic baggage.

If all this sounds less than flattering, it isn’t because Chabal has written a hatchet job. On the contrary: The Age of Hobsbawm is admiring of the historian’s accomplishments while mercifully free of the emotional overinvestments he inspired in earlier generations. The absence of tedious Cold War moralism — alternately prosecutorial or tortured on such questions as Hobsbawm’s failure to leave the party after 1956 or his enjoyment of establishment privileges — is refreshing. Chabal offers a decidedly twenty-first century perspective, concerned more with explaining the global phenomenon that was Hobsbawm than judging the man or seeking to revive his ideas. But the line between demythologization and deflation is thin. Turning a high-resolution lens on the sausage-making of academic advancement and intellectual reputation-building is bound to leave any subject diminished.

While some of the details will be familiar to those who have read Richard Evans’s 2019 biography, Chabal’s cool-eyed appraisal repeatedly brings the legend down to earth. As a supervisor of graduate students, Hobsbawm was usually inattentive, veering into downright hostility to approaches he disliked: women’s and feminist histories foremost among them. He never made peace with the New Left sensibility that took gender and race as seriously as class. For all his interest in cultural production — an enthusiasm shaped, though not straitjacketed, by the Marxist catechism of base and superstructure — his tastes were fusty. He found jazz a worthwhile topic in the 1950s only insofar as it met his standards for popular authenticity, which meant embodying black folk traditions while retaining mass commercial appeal. For a man whose aesthetics were enduringly forged in the same 1930s youth as his politics, Miles Davis and John Coltrane missed the mark. As for the actually existing popular music of rock and roll, Hobsbawm thought Elvis Presley “peculiarly unappealing” and wrote dismissively of the Beatles that “anyone can produce that sound.”

Old-fashioned in some ways, Hobsbawm was extremely well matched to his time in others. The success of his books reflected their timeliness. The massive expansion of higher education on both sides of the Atlantic created demand for accessible introductions to economic history, such as his Industry and Empire (1968), and modern Europe, covered in the famous tetralogy that began with The Age of Revolution (1962). The “paperback revolution” described by historian Peter Mandler solidified the market for serious nonfiction in affordable editions. Not least, Marxism enjoyed enormous intellectual cachet — and a mass following — in societies as disparate as Italy, India, and Brazil. The Eurocentrism of the Ages volumes, so conspicuous in retrospect, mattered less at a time when many of the most pressing Marxist debates — about the demise of feudalism, the advent of industrial production, and the immiseration of workers — were being waged on the terrain of British history.

Little wonder that Hobsbawm’s work repeatedly circled back to what he saw as the formation of mass society in the late nineteenth century. Universal education, rising literacy, new communication technologies, a popular press: these were not just the preconditions for nationalism, democracy, and ideological politics in the fin de siècle. They were also the foundations, in a more distant way, of Hobsbawm’s success in the literary marketplace. The volume devoted to the late nineteenth century, The Age of Empire (1987), marked a turning point in the series, arguing that the forces that destabilized and ultimately destroyed bourgeois society emerged from the triumphant capitalist order it had built. Hobsbawm doubtless savored the irony, in his own career, of leveraging the commercial incentives of the book business to deliver left-wing history to hundreds of thousands of readers.

Particularly in the Ages series, it is difficult to disentangle Marxism from other historiographical influences. It is also true that the tetralogy is at its least convincing when it hews most closely to orthodox Marxism. Yes, the elegant architecture of the series derives from the interlocking advance of a new mode of production (industrial capitalism), a new social grouping (the bourgeoisie), and a new ideology (liberalism). But this master narrative strains to meet the facts at crucial moments. Hobsbawm’s interpretation of the French Revolution — one half of the “dual revolution” that kicks off the series — in the strict class terms of a “bourgeois revolution” was outdated almost as soon as the ink was dry. The risk of historiographical obsolescence became more acute as the interval between volumes lengthened; by the 1980s, historians were questioning whether the bourgeoisie anywhere in nineteenth-century Europe was really so triumphant in the face of what Arno Mayer called “the persistence of the old regime.” At the same time, as Chabal points out, Hobsbawm’s decision to elevate political principles of liberty and equality to the same explanatory rank as the Industrial Revolution marked a bold departure from strictly materialist analysis.

It is something of a cliché to describe Hobsbawm as cosmopolitan because of his birth in Alexandria, childhood in Vienna, and adolescence in Berlin. The label fits best as a statement of his role as an intellectual intermediary, bringing elements of the French Annales school into mainstream Anglophone historiography at a time when few others were doing so. I am less sure than Chabal that “total history” is the right term for the Ages series; Fernand Braudel’s The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II (1949) and Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie’s Montaillou (1975) traded specific geographic boundaries for depths of environmental and anthropological texture not captured by the ostensibly global scale on which Hobsbawm was working.

Marxist annalistes such as Ernest Labrousse, who in 1955 issued a prominent call for a history of the nineteenth-century bourgeoisie, represent a more obvious influence. But if Hobsbawm and the other towering figure of his generation of British historians, E. P. Thompson, both subordinated high politics to social history, Hobsbawm’s route to that destination — reflected in the pages of tables and charts that adorned many of his books — was paved with the quantitative data that the Annales valued so highly. Without ever bogging down the fluent prose of the Ages series, price cycles and export volumes provided the materialist grounding for Hobsbawm’s confident pronouncements on everything from urban planning and domestic architecture to music, painting, and literature.

That empiricist brio, Chabal shows, might be the most British thing about Hobsbawm. He was a product of the Oxbridge system in his talent for generalizing from well-chosen details, though probably no one could do it as artfully. A flair for what Hobsbawm himself called haute vulgarisation served him well as a university lecturer and is the reason that the Ages books remain so readable today. Unlike Thompson, Hobsbawm did not forsake high culture along with high politics, and his sympathetic interest in popular protest did not foreclose writing about the likes of Ludwig van Beethoven, Honoré de Balzac, and Albert Einstein. Hobsbawm’s identification with “history from below,” more pronounced in some works than others, was always more equivocal than for some of his peers — perhaps because, at least to some degree, he absorbed and accepted the cultural values of the Bildungsbürgertum.

Chabal emphasizes the critical edge of Hobsbawm’s take on the superficiality and artificiality of the bourgeois world. But there was also nostalgia, or at least ambivalence, in Hobsbawm’s attitude to the class that dominated his magnum opus. In the introduction to The Age of Empire, the historian’s affective connection to the era in which his parents came of age inspired some of his most lyrical lines:

blockquote.p: For all of us there is a twilight zone between history and memory. . . . For individual human beings this zone stretches from the point where living family traditions or memories begin . . . to the end of infancy, when public and private destinies are recognized as inseparable. . . . It is itself an incoherent, incompletely perceived image of the past, sometimes more shadowy, sometimes apparently precise, always transmitted by a mixture of learning and second-hand memory shaped by public and private tradition. For it is still part of us, but no longer quite within our personal reach.

div.p: The tantalizing proximity, yet ultimate inaccessibility, of those years before 1914 is especially poignant because Hobsbawm’s parents died young. But there is a hint of social as well as personal loss, a longing for the solidity of the bourgeois order swept away by the war. The final volume in the series, The Age of Extremes (1994), has an unmoored quality as violent events overwhelm structures and processes in the maelstrom of what Hobsbawm termed “the short twentieth century.” The better companion for the first three Ages volumes is arguably Peter Gay’s The Bourgeois Experience (1984–1998), the work of another Jewish émigré from Central Europe, born six years after Hobsbawm, though with Sigmund Freud rather than Karl Marx as the theoretical lodestar. In different ways, both works are about the “fragility” and the “tenuous grip” of bourgeois dominance (to borrow from Chabal’s gloss on Hobsbawm).

The twentieth century might have appeared less disjunctive in Hobsbawm’s telling if colonial violence had featured more prominently all along. The treatment of the Haitian Revolution as an afterthought in The Age of Revolution is symptomatic of the series as a whole: the world-systems weighting of “center” and “periphery” applies not only to capitalist development but to ideas, experiences, and people as well. Even The Age of Empire fails to live up to its title in large part because Hobsbawm leans so heavily on the Hobsonian-Leninist model of imperialism as an outgrowth of monopoly capitalism. It is a book about the “apotheosis” and “destruction” of the bourgeoisie, Chabal writes, while the human catastrophe of imperial conquest is reduced to the abstract “terms of a political and historiographical debate that needed to be settled.” Even on Hobsbawm’s own terms, this focus on Europe represents a missed opportunity, because the vulnerability of the bourgeoisie was nowhere more acute than in the colonial outposts that strove to replicate European society far from home.

Though he famously refused to join Thompson and others in leaving the Communist Party of Great Britain in 1956, Hobsbawm emerged from the shattering of its intellectual milieu with a more flexible and questioning attitude to the party line, producing some of his most interesting work as a consequence. His 1959 book Primitive Rebels took seriously the political aspirations of peasant uprisings far removed from the industrial proletariat privileged by Marxist theory. His later work on nationalism discussed ideological regimes of collective identity with only limited reference to material causes.

Where Hobsbawm evolved least was almost certainly in his Eurocentrism: an imperfect term, not least because it masks the novelty of his attention to the ways that global and imperial forces remade Europe. It would be difficult to imagine Sven Beckert’s “war capitalism” or Kenneth Pomeranz’s “ghost acres,” for instance, without the pioneering argument of Industry and Empire, which linked the onset of the Industrial Revolution to the demand boost of imperial expansion. Of course, Hobsbawm’s books will continue to be read for the sheer artistry of their craft: the subordination of narrative to structure, the fluency in shifting between macro and micro scales, the promiscuous variety of sources, the plain yet vigorous expository prose.

Yet his reluctance to wrestle with topics that most historians today would consider central — genocide and decolonization — shows that the path for history after Hobsbawm is not only a matter of geographical rebalancing. Rather than writing Europe out of the story, we must write about it differently: no longer as the cradle of an immanent logic of history but as the cockpit of a violent, acquisitive, sometimes irrational, and often unpredictable project of domination whose consequences we have yet to fully grasp.
