entry.title: The Bosses’ Oldest Dream

div.p: The English inventor Charles Babbage is best remembered for his work designing the foundations for all digital computers with Ada Lovelace in the nineteenth century. What’s lesser known is why he wanted to build them. In the decades leading up to the British Empire’s abolition of slavery in the West Indies in 1833 (which Babbage supported), there was a serious question of how to get free and rebellious industrial workers to produce enough to sustain the empire. Babbage’s answer was to surveil workers and divide their efforts into standardized, measurable tasks — a project he saw as a necessary step on the way to automating labor entirely.

Babbage didn’t invent these methods, as Meredith Whittaker, an artificial intelligence scholar who coled Google’s 2018 walkout, writes in a Logic(s) essay. Similar technologies of labor control were developed first on plantations to extract maximum labor from enslaved people, with management guides routinely circulating among British capitalists. “Babbage’s proto-Taylorist ideas on how to discipline workers are inextricably connected to the calculating engines he spent his life attempting to build,” Whittaker writes. Automation gave bosses a tool to replace striking workers and provided a disciplinary check, in Babbage’s words, “against the inattention, the idleness, or the dishonesty of human agents.”

There’s a neat alpha and omega quality to computing: its ultimate effort, the Obsoleting Project — the industry’s drive to build machines that can do all our jobs — rhymes with its earliest. Should they work as intended, those machines would act as the tireless, pliant, cheap workers that bosses could previously only dream of. From Babbage to Bezos, managers have always resented the various ways that humans aren’t optimized for output — and therefore, their bottom line.

For bosses, cost savings alone are only part of the attraction. Automation also weakens workers’ bargaining power and is used to make organizing even harder. After workers alleged Amazon used algorithmic management to surveil and stifle protected labor organizing, Stanford Law Lecturer Seema N. Patel told The Guardian that AI lets employers discipline hundreds of thousands of workers “in a way that no human manager or group of managers could even do.”
“You feel like you’re in prison,” Wendy Taylor, an Amazon packer, said. “They know every move you make, when you’re working, when you’re not working.”
Of course, Amazon is also leading the charge on replacing workers entirely.

Yoshua Bengio is the most-cited living scientist thanks to his foundational contributions to deep learning. “I’m talking to a lot of CEOs around the world,” he told me, “and they’ll automate [jobs] as fast as they possibly can.” Indeed, a 2025 World Economic Forum survey of more than one thousand large employers found more than 40 percent planned to reduce their workforce as a result of automation by 2030.

Companies are also creating more wealth with fewer people than ever. Per employee, the world’s most valuable companies in recent decades were worth anywhere from $3.5 million to as much as $30 million. Nvidia? More than $100 million. Pure AI firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI have pushed the trend even further, with ratios between $140 million and $167 million.

This surge in AI-driven wealth concentration builds on a decades-long rise in inequality. As the economists Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman have shown, inequality levels in the United States are the highest they’ve been since the 1920s. If machines can truly substitute for human labor across the board, the result could look like a worldwide game of musical chairs, where your economic position is determined by whatever wealth you happened to have at the moment your work stopped being worth paying for.
Looking at this data, AI appears less a bolt from the blue than the next — and perhaps final — frontier in the endless pursuit of profit.
It probably comes as little surprise to you that many capitalists want to automate their workers away. But can they?

The question is difficult to answer definitively. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei sounded the alarm in mid-2025, predicting what Axios dubbed a “white-collar bloodbath.” AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and spike overall unemployment to 10 to 20 percent in the next one to five years, he told the publication. Of course, to skeptics, the CEO of an AI company warning that its technology would be so effective it would soon replace human workers was nothing more than a savvy earned media campaign. But that’s hard to square with more recent reporting that OpenAI blocked its economists from publishing research that showed its technology was displacing jobs.

By 2025, signs of AI’s deleterious effects on the workforce appeared to be everywhere. Rising unemployment for college graduates, dips in job postings, and dramatic Big Tech layoffs were all pointing the same way, and software engineer hiring in particular cratered. People were quick to attribute the drop to AI.

However, as keen observers noted, the plunge in hiring coincided more neatly with the Fed’s increases to interest rates than with the rise of ChatGPT, which didn’t become much of a coder until after net hiring had (barely) resumed. Generative AI rose to prominence at around the same time as today’s turbulent macroeconomic and political conditions, making it fiendishly difficult to explain changes. Anecdata in the form of news stories about young people struggling to find programming jobs won’t cut it.
I hate to say it, but this sounds like a job for economists.

In 2024, when Daron Acemoglu — who would go on to share that year’s Nobel Prize in economics — predicted the labor market effects of AI over the next decade, people took notice. Against Goldman Sachs and McKinsey predictions that AI would add trillions to GDP, he expected a nothingburger, forecasting that US GDP would only be around 1 percent higher in ten years due to AI.

Economists mostly don’t believe there’s any real chance AI could put most people out of work anytime soon, Stanford economics postdoc Phil Trammell told me, but Acemoglu’s view is even “more pessimistic than the mainstream.”

On the opposite end of the spectrum is Anton Korinek, a University of Virginia economist on leave at Anthropic since March, who uses standard economic models to look at what might happen if firms can effectively turn capital into more labor. Assuming full automation is reached in twenty years (“baseline AGI”), he and his PhD student Donghyun Suh predict the economy would double over the subsequent decade. If it’s possible in five years (“aggressive AGI”), they predict a tripling of GDP by 2034 — ten times faster growth than the business-as-usual scenario. “However,” they write, “wages collapse as the economy approaches full automation.”

“Economists have been telling the rest of the world for the past 200 years that we shouldn’t worry about automation,” Korinek told me, “because if you destroy some jobs, the economy always creates new ones.” That was true in the past, he acknowledged, but only because “there were always things that only humans could do.” Indeed, there are more people than ever before, with more jobs than ever before, even after more than two centuries of automation. However, we’ve never had a machine that can actually make labor. (Korinek has separately clarified he’s not predicting imminent AGI himself, but rather using traditional economics to show what would happen if the predictions of AI experts like Geoffrey Hinton actually came to pass.)

Economic forecasts are notoriously sensitive to their underlying assumptions. Acemoglu’s 2024 paper uses mainstream ways to measure a task’s automation potential. But when it comes to AI’s capabilities, he takes a distinctly conservative approach, assuming they won’t significantly advance beyond GPT-4’s, which was the state of the art at the time.

Trammell told me that the difference between the Acemoglu and Korinek camps comes down to “whether the economic impacts of AI over the next ten years will be mainly about the diffusion of what AI could already do as of a year ago versus the things it becomes able to do over the next ten years.”
That’s not really an economics question, Trammell said. “It’s a question about technological forecasting. I think reasonable people can disagree about it. But it’s also not Daron’s wheelhouse.”

In September 2025, I interviewed Acemoglu for a Nobel Foundation panel during the United Nations General Assembly. To my surprise, he said he was going to “stick to his guns.” In a late 2024 interview, he had argued that the productivity story depends on the technology creating genuinely new tasks and new products, and he doesn’t see the industry’s current focus delivering much of that within a decade. He expects near-term gains to concentrate in relatively “easy-to-learn” white-collar tasks, while jobs that rely on tacit judgment, social interaction, and hard-to-verify outcomes remain far less exposed.

It is true that, even years after the release of ChatGPT, it’s been hard to find evidence that AI is actually killing jobs. An October 2025 Yale study using the standard dataset for labor economists, the US Current Population Survey (CPS), found that “currently, measures of exposure, automation, and augmentation show no sign of being related to changes in employment or unemployment.” Also in October, when I asked Korinek about the data to date, he admitted that we only have “tiny little bits of empirical evidence that are not rising to the level of transformativeness.” So, “if you say I’m an honest evidence-bound economist, it’s still fair to say that the evidence doesn’t suggest that this is different from any prior technological revolution.”

But focusing on whole occupations may miss the early signs of automation. This is where three Stanford economists stepped in with a groundbreaking paper in August 2025. Rather than rely on traditional government sources like CPS, which offer a useful — but bird’s-eye — view of employment changes, they got their hands on data from a payroll processor, allowing them to zoom in on trends too subtle to spot otherwise. Spoiler: the anecdotes were a real sign that the white-collar bloodbath was already well underway, and like the 1918 flu, it claimed young people most.

With payroll data going back to 2021, the authors split professions into six age cohorts, starting with twenty-two- to twenty-five-year-olds, and bucketed jobs by AI exposure using the same metric as Acemoglu. The most exposed were in fields like programming and customer service.

After controlling for interest rates, pandemic-era overhiring, and other factors, the data tells no clear story at first. Even for the youngest, most AI-exposed workers, relative employment bounced around for years, declining as much as 6 percent in 2022 before recovering to zero in mid-2024. But then it falls off a cliff, plummeting 16 percent in just over a year, with little sign of stopping.

By late 2025, the macro data looked consistent with this story. The US economy grew at 4.3 percent in the third quarter — the fastest in two years — while job creation averaged an anemic 51,000 per month. Joseph Brusuelas, the chief economist at the accounting firm RSM, writes, “The great decoupling of jobs and growth will take some explaining to the American public.” The Stanford paper offers one compelling explanation.

Korinek worries that we’re heading toward something more fundamental than a rough patch for entry-level coders. “The main economic risk under AI,” he told me, “is that it will fundamentally undermine labor, that it will lead to essentially a large part of the population becoming losers of this technology.” He observed that wage labor was “basically a construct of the industrial age” — one not likely to survive long term under AGI, where, by default, he expected labor to “experience a very significant devaluation.”

The rise of automation in the United States is happening after decades of declining union density, with just 6 percent of private sector workers belonging to one. Currently, labor automation mostly doesn’t look like mass layoffs; instead the Stanford paper suggests firms will increasingly avoid hiring anyone they might be able to automate — a group that will grow larger as AI improves.
And since AI labor is typically orders of magnitude cheaper than the human variety, substitution doesn’t require that AI be as good, just good enough.

After years reporting on the Obsoleting Project, I’ve found that lawmakers won’t stop it unless we make them. The industry has captured them, and they were already catastrophically insulated from what the public wants. What has slowed automation down, where anything has, is workers organizing.

One place where bosses tried — but largely failed — to use automation to reduce labor power was in scriptwriting. To better understand how, I spoke to Ellen Stutzman, the chief negotiator for the Writers Guild of America (WGA) 2023 strike. She told me that AI concerns emerged organically from what members were already experiencing: a speedup. As streaming replaced broadcast television over the preceding fifteen years, studios shifted from fewer shows with twenty-two-episode seasons to more shows with just eight-episode seasons, asking writers to do more work in less time for less money. The writers were already going into the strike seeking contractual minimums on staffing levels and time to do jobs. So when ChatGPT arrived, it looked like the natural progression of that trend. “It’s like one writer with an AI system doing an entire season,” Stutzman said, “or eventually no writers.”

The WGA didn’t go into bargaining demanding a ban on AI. Instead, it wanted restrictions on how the technology was used, namely for AI-generated material to be treated the way Wikipedia articles were — as research, not writing. If a studio hands a writer AI-generated material, the writer should still get full credit and compensation. Whatever the machine spits out doesn’t count as literary material under the contract. And writers shouldn’t be forced to use AI tools. That last one mattered, she said, because members’ views ran the whole spectrum: “People like David Simon, who was on the negotiating committee, who I think said, ‘I would rather put a gun in my mouth than use AI.’”

It was only on the final weekend before the contract deadline, Stutzman said, that the studios were willing to say anything at all about AI. At that point, they finally pointed to language in the existing collective bargaining agreement saying that a “writer” is a human being and told the guild that, at least on paper, AI could not be credited as the writer. But they stressed that they did not want to limit how they might use the technology in practice.

This coincided with concerns over studios using AI to scan actors to create “synthetic performers” for background shots. The Screen Actors Guild–American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) launched its own strike a few months later, in which the use of digital replicas became a key sticking point.

It took a five-month strike to get the protections writers wanted, and Stutzman is clear-eyed about the limits of what they achieved: the WGA has no power over any AI company. “What we can do in a collective bargaining agreement is regulate our employers,” she said, “but OpenAI is not our employer.” The companies that scraped writers’ work to train their models remain beyond the guild’s direct reach — a problem the WGA is now trying to address through litigation and legislation.

Against this bleak backdrop, I asked Stutzman what other automation-exposed workers could learn from their experience. She didn’t hesitate. “It’s the same lesson I have on everything, which is about collective power,” she said. “If you want to push back, if you want to regulate AI, if you want to make it a tool that you use versus one you’re being replaced with — it’s all about collective action.”

entry.title: A Decade of Bernie Sanders’s Transformation of America

div.p: Over the past decade since his first presidential run, no one has done more to reshape the American left than Bernie Sanders. He is the most influential left-wing leader this country has seen since the 1960s, if not longer.

While Sanders’s political career began decades earlier, his influence took on national dimensions ten years ago, when Sanders first campaigned for president against Hillary Clinton in the Democratic primary. He lost that campaign, but few losses have looked so much like a victory. Clinton has no political heirs openly claiming her legacy; indeed, today’s technocratic centrists squirm away from the association. Meanwhile, Sanders has dozens of self-professed acolytes at the federal level, hundreds or even thousands at the state and local levels, and an organization in the Democratic Socialists of America that, though he has never been a member, has grown from obscurity to 120,000 members since he first ran.

Bernie Sanders’s first presidential campaign, then, is a significant event in twenty-first century American politics and the broader history of the American left, and its ten-year anniversary is a notable milestone. But Sanders himself hasn’t marked the occasion. Unlike most politicians, he demurs from telling his own story or touting his achievements. He’s also busy, playing a leading role in demanding artificial intelligence regulation and ending the war in Iran, with the next fight and the one after that.
That laser focus on the present is why we love Bernie; it also means that commemorating and reflecting on the campaign that changed everything falls to us.

At the top of any accounting of Sanders’s achievements since 2016 is the wave of young socialist elected officials he has inspired. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was a volunteer organizer for Sanders’s 2016 campaign, which she credits with motivating her to run for office. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has called Sanders “the single most influential political figure in my life” and has said it was “Bernie’s campaign for the presidency in 2016 that gave me the language of democratic socialism to describe my politics.”

Sanders’s protégés in Congress now span two generations. There are the upperclassmen elected around 2018, including Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar, and Rashida Tlaib. And pending November confirmation in their deep-blue districts, there’s now an incoming freshman class including Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, while several other Sanders acolytes, chief among them Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, are fighting through their general elections with a good shot at victory.

Valdez best summarized this cohort’s indebtedness to Sanders when she said, “Three things made me a democratic socialist: sh–y jobs, the labor movement, and Bernie Sanders’s runs for president. His political revolution changed my life — and showed millions of Americans what’s possible when working people organize.”
Sanders’s influence, however, is hardly restricted to office-seekers. His political orientation has reshaped the culture and strategic orientation of the American left as a whole.

To appreciate how, recall what that culture looked like before he arrived. From the Battle of Seattle in 1999 through Occupy Wall Street in 2011, the American left was dominated by horizontalism, an anarchist-inflected politics that distrusted not only politicians and parties but mass politics itself. The Occupy-era left was suspicious of formal leadership, considered demands a concession to the system, and rarely organized itself beyond the affinity group or temporary action committees.

The mobilizations of this period produced indelible images and genuinely radicalized participants, but they left behind no institutions capable of seriously contesting power. Meanwhile, those progressives who did continue to wage fights within the Democratic Party did so timidly and without ambition, failing to advance a robust legislative program and inspiring moral vision. Sanders offered an exit from both culs-de-sac.

By running for president on a far-reaching program of reforms that were coherent and achievable but also highly audacious and transformative, he demonstrated that the Left could flourish by articulating clear demands and waging campaigns for Democratic Party nominations that were mostly independent of Democratic Party leadership. He showed that we could seek majorities and contest for power rather than just protest it — and that millions of ordinary people, mostly indifferent to the subcultural preoccupations of the already-existing activist left, would respond when we did.

img.alt: Bernie Sanders delivers remarks in a Brooklyn park during his 2016 presidential campaign.

figure.figcaption: Bernie speaks at Transmitter Park in Brooklyn, New York, on April 8, 2016. (Timothy Krause / CC BY 2.0)

div.p: If horizontalism was the radical left’s dominant tendency when Sanders arrived, identity politics was its successor in the decade that followed. The Right makes no distinction between the two emergent politics of the 2010s, Sanders-style democratic socialism and “wokeness.” In reality, however, Bernie Sanders has provided an alternate example for a left that otherwise finds it difficult to avoid the seductions of identity-based oppression rankings, elaborate deference pageantry, and shallow representational concerns. A universalist at heart, Sanders instead has modeled a politics genuinely progressive on civil rights and social equality that nonetheless declines the invitation to the culture wars, fixing its attention instead on what unites the broad working class rather than on the infinite ways it can be subdivided.

That Sanders’s politics, forged in the crucible of the Free Speech and Civil Rights movements, remained wholly intact through the Left’s darkest decades is a testament to his idiosyncratic personality as much as his political convictions. Through sheer force of will, he has served as a bridge between the 1960s and our time. We’re lucky that a veteran of the nation’s last great left upsurge was still around to guide a new generation of democratic socialists — and that he had spent decades in office sorting what earlier generations got right from what they got wrong.

There’s no one like Bernie Sanders. He remains singular today, even among the crop of leaders and activists who strive to emulate him. His obdurate universalism, unique and even comical ability to stay on message, and unyielding focus on issues of real importance to the long project of class struggle remain aspirational qualities. Society has not evolved past the need for Bernie Sanders.

To mark the decade anniversary of Sanders’s first presidential campaign, we will be publishing a number of articles in the coming days by Jacobin contributors and contemporary socialist leaders reflecting on how the American left has changed since Bernie first ran. These articles will cover his impact on socialist organizations, his part in the still-unfinished effort to revitalize the labor movement, personal essays by socialist elected officials on his influence on them, and more.

Though he’s far from finished remaking American politics, Sanders has already left a profound legacy that will not recede when he does eventually exit the public stage. Above all, he has broken the spell of demoralization that had settled over the American left, and over the working class itself. He has rekindled in millions of Americans the belief that things can change — that domination can be challenged, inequality overturned, injustice repaired, and power structures transformed in the interests of the many, not just the wealthy few.

entry.title: Obama’s Monument to Empty Liberalism

div.p: “When I first saw it, I was like, ‘It’s a block.’” Woodlawn resident Linda Spears had been watching the construction of the Obama Foundation’s sprawling campus from her condo overlooking Jackson Park in Chicago, but it wasn’t until opening weekend, when the barriers came down, that she finally went inside. Sitting on a bench near the Barack Obama Presidential Center’s playground, she recited the former president’s 2015 speech on the fiftieth anniversary of the Selma to Montgomery march from memory, as if echoing the words that appeared on the facade behind us.

Spears explained that the museum tower at the Obama Presidential Center had actually been designed to resemble four hands reaching upward. She pressed her hands against those of a young woman beside her, as if playing patty-cake. “It’s like we’re all coming together,” she said.

I saw this demonstration of the four hands many times during opening weekend, literally gesturing toward Obama’s vision of the center as “not just a monument to my presidency” but “a tribute to all the people and the forces and the community that helped to make this so special.” It’s an inspirational story every American liberal knows by heart: Obama arrived on the South Side of Chicago as a wayward twenty-three-year-old in a junky used car and left as the president of the United States. He envisioned the sprawling Obama Presidential Center campus as a thank-you gift to the city that created him, complete with a playground, a public library branch, gardens, and spaces for democratic education in a basement “forum.”

On opening weekend, visitors lined up for paletas and Obama-themed merchandise at stands encouraging them to “bring change home.” They nodded along to Stevie Wonder’s live performance while inspecting hot peppers in the garden and wrote notes to Obama on index cards in the Forum basement and pinned them to the wall. Even on Sunday, when thunderstorms thinned out the crowds, a DJ shouted over the promenade, “We may be small in number, but we can make an impact.” Meanwhile, a cluster of visitors with umbrellas wobbled through the Electric Slide.

Nowhere had I seen so many slogans: a T-shirt featuring Parks and Recreation’s Ron Swanson with “I regret nothing” in Impact typeface, Future voter pins for the kids. Some seemed to be handmade — a group visiting from Mississippi had matching traffic-cone-orange shirts with Obama’s head superimposed on a photo of the Obama Center campus; the words “where we come to be inspired and change” appeared in white italics across the bottom. Another woman wore a white shirt with a wanted poster featuring Obama’s face. Above him read the headline “Have you seen this man? If so, can you please let him back into the White House?” Visitors would also see these kinds of handmade slogans and signs in the museum itself, relics from the civil rights movement and Harold Washington’s mayoral campaign as well as a display of 440 buttons from Obama’s 2008 presidential campaign — German-Americans for Obama, UAW for Obama–Biden, Vote Hope.

The Obama museum’s celebration of the power of ordinary people may ring hollow, given the high-profile donors required to fund its $850 million budget. It’s difficult to sustain the cognitive dissonance of seeing an Occupy Wall Street display funded in part by Goldman Sachs and Bank of America, or stomach an exhibit about labor organizing after having wandered past a sign thanking Jeff Bezos.

Even more ironic is the Obama Foundation’s apparent hostility to community organizers on the South Side. After the foundation announced in 2016 that the center would be built in Jackson Park, local faith organizations, tenant groups, and neighborhood associations formed a coalition to negotiate a community benefits agreement (CBA), a legally binding contract intended to protect Woodlawn residents from displacement. The foundation made a series of vague, voluntary commitments to community demands but chafed against the request to formalize them into a legally enforceable agreement. During a 2017 meeting, organizer and now alderwoman Jeanette Taylor asked Obama directly why he would not sign a CBA. “I was a community organizer,” Obama replied. “I know the neighborhood. I know that the minute you start saying, ‘Well, we’re thinking about signing something that will determine who’s getting jobs and contracts and this and that’ . . . next thing I know, I’ve got twenty organizations coming out of the woodwork.” It did not go over well. “He’s forgotten who he is,” Taylor later told a reporter. “He forgot the community got him where he is.”

When Obama was elected to the Illinois State Senate in 1996, his wife, Michelle, said, “Barack is not a politician first and foremost. He’s a community activist exploring the viability of politics to make change.” In 2008, Sarah Palin mocked Obama’s lack of government experience from the Republican National Convention stage, sneering that “I guess a small-town mayor is sort of like a community organizer, except that you have actual responsibilities.” In his ascent to the Oval Office, Obama brought the question of what it means to be an organizer to the center of American politics. In the form of a near-billion-dollar museum, it seems that he has finally given his answer.

On the third floor of the Obama museum, under a spotlight, is a magazine open to an article entitled “Why Organize? Problems and Promise in the Inner City.” In it, a twenty-seven-year-old Obama reflects on his time on the South Side. He begins the essay with an anecdote in which a public school administrative aide pulls him aside on a “bleak January morning” to ask why “a bright young man like [him] would go to college, get that degree and become a community organizer.” In the gentle, even-keeled mode that would eventually become his signature style, he argued that political and economic representation for black Chicagoans — in the form of elected officials like Harold Washington and “increased hiring of black contractors and corporate managers, or Buy Black campaigns” — had been largely “symbolic.” Only through organizing could the South Side harness its “internal productive capacities” toward systemic change.

It is difficult to reconcile “Why Organize?” with the building in which it lives. The Obama Foundation celebrates the strategies that Obama had himself dismissed in 1988. Press releases proclaim the museum as a totem of Obama’s symbolic victory as the first black president and an engine of economic development on the South Side, “supporting thousands of jobs during and after construction.” The museum’s exhibits breeze past these contradictions. To wrap up Obama’s time as a community organizer, text strewn on the wall explains that “victories were rare,” and “Barack decided he could make a bigger difference in his community if he ran for elected office.”

Filling in these gaps is a series of documents that line the walls. A couple years after “Why Organize?” was originally published in 1988, it appeared in an anthology, After Alinsky: Community Organizing in Illinois, reflecting on the legacy of Saul Alinsky, a towering figure in Chicago organizing. Alinsky tried to systematize the ad hoc techniques he encountered during a lifetime of organizing in Back of the Yards into a set of replicable methods, which he listed in his book Rules for Radicals (on sale at the Obama Center bookshop). Alinsky hoped to bring unions, churches, and other local groups together in a “People’s Organization” that could represent a neighborhood in perpetuity rather than wilting after the end of a particular campaign. At the age of twenty-three, after seeing a help wanted ad in The New York Times, Obama joined an attempt at one such organization, the Developing Communities Project (DCP), a coalition of Catholic parishes on Chicago’s far South Side. Obama’s bosses at the DCP, one of whom described himself as an Alinsky “disciple,” were trained in Alinsky’s methods. The museum displays a fax pinned to a wall, a lesson on Alinsky’s approach to coalition building, with Obama’s handwritten marginalia, notes like “self-interest” and “systemic,” in careful cursive.

The museum includes little information about what Obama worked on at the DCP, save for a newspaper clipping from 1988. A grainy black-and-white photo shows a young Obama speaking to a couple of frowning white men, residents of Hegewisch, a southeastern Chicago neighborhood that borders Indiana. Hegewisch is enclosed by what activist Hazel M. Johnson called the “toxic doughnut,” a ring of landfills, highways, sewage treatment facilities, and chemical plants that pollute the surrounding neighborhoods. In his last months at the DCP, Obama was on a task force to prevent the development of new landfills through regulatory blockades. After he left for Harvard Law School later that year, the campaign won a moratorium on new waste sites. But fifty dumps and more than one hundred industrial plants remained, managed by both city agencies and private companies. The toxic doughnut exists to this day.

In “Why Organize?,” Obama wrote that Chicago was haunted by the “skeletons” of these campaigns, dismayed to find that community organizing at the DCP felt more like cutting heads off a hydra than the David-and-Goliath fights he had romanticized before he took the job. Still, Obama had not abandoned Alinsky’s dream of the “People’s Organization” that could buoy movements across long-haul fights against overlapping public and private institutions. The future president wondered if he could “rework old models” of organizing like Alinsky’s “to fit new realities,” allowing community organizers, elected officials, and private companies to work hand in hand.

The result of such a proposal was 2008’s Obama for America (OFA). OFA sought to imbue a presidential campaign with the energy of community organizing. Washington strategists set the agenda from the top down, but volunteers were encouraged to personalize it. Marshall Ganz, an activist and academic who helped shape the campaign’s organizing model, designed and led “Camp Obama,” volunteer training boot camps that were essentially storytelling workshops. Whether canvassing door-to-door or training new recruits, volunteers were instructed to move from “self” to “us” to “now”: beginning with a personal story, connecting it to the shared values of a community, and concluding with a call to action. Obama’s eventual victory was fueled by one of the largest volunteer organizations in American political history. The 440 campaign buttons lining a semicircle at the center of the museum’s third floor each represent five thousand campaign volunteers. Obama attempted to make OFA’s grassroots power permanent, transforming it first into Organizing for America (a project housed within the Democratic National Committee) and later into the independent nonprofit Organizing for Action. But the experiment proved difficult to sustain. Fundraising and staffing declined after 2012, and by 2018, Organizing for Action had merged into a redistricting committee before fizzling out altogether.

Although it says little about Obama for America or Organizing for Action as institutions, the Obama Center Museum perfectly embodies Marshall Ganz’s three-act canvassing structure. The emotional climax of the campaign floor features a video of people around the world celebrating Obama’s election, complete with a box of tissues provided on a nearby chair. The galleries focused on the presidency years continue this move from “self” to “us” by showing the everyday people who benefited from Obama’s policies. There is the framed letter from Natoma Canfield, an Ohio cleaner who gained health insurance under the Affordable Care Act, and the wedding ring and marriage certificate of Jim Obergefell, the lead plaintiff in the Supreme Court case that legalized same-sex marriage nationwide. In the last few galleries, visitors are invited to design a campaign button of their own on an elaborate digital display before finally ascending to the “Sky Room” to look out at the city and reflect on their own capacity for action.

But the Obama Presidential Center wants to do more than inspire visitors — it aims to be a civic institution capable of reshaping Woodlawn through a grab bag of community initiatives. It’s not as strange an ambition as it sounds. From its origins, the American presidential library has occupied an ambiguous space between public and private. When Franklin D. Roosevelt went looking for a way to institutionalize the preservation of presidential documents, he used the model of the National Gallery, which was then under construction, to structure his own archive: a private foundation would construct the building, while the federal government would maintain the records therein. He called this institution a library, a friendlier, folksier term than the imposing “archive,” with a clear connection to the public good. But as presidential libraries have ballooned in both size and construction costs in recent years — and become opportunities for elite fundraising — this system has been subject to increased scrutiny, as former presidents have saddled the federal government with the responsibility of maintaining increasingly palatial monuments to themselves.

The Obama Foundation tried to skirt these controversies by cleaving the museum itself from the archive. Unlike traditional presidential libraries, the Obama Presidential Center contains no federally operated presidential records. Instead, the National Archives digitized and maintains Obama’s presidential records, while the Obama Foundation operates the museum independently.

But the foundation has muddied the waters between private and public in other ways. In 2014, Mayor Rahm Emanuel, who once served as Obama’s chief of staff, allowed the Obama Foundation to appropriate acres of Jackson Park to build the presidential center. City officials put more than $123 million toward infrastructure improvements surrounding it. Resource appropriation on this scale was not uncommon for a presidential library under construction. The Commonwealth of Massachusetts purchased land from Boston’s transit authority for the JFK Library, while Lyndon B. Johnson’s library was constructed on public land donated by the University of Texas at Austin. Rather than going to war against the tangled web of public and private institutions he faced as a community organizer, Obama joined them. With a ninety-nine-year contract from the city and over $1 billion in assets, the Obama Presidential Center can make greater claims to permanence than OFA or the DCP ever could. Perhaps in that luxurious time frame, it can make good on its promise to transform Jackson Park into a “living, working center for citizenship.”

Obama told The New Republic in 2007 that “people’s hopes and dreams and their ideals and their values were just as important in organizing as people’s self-interest.” His foundation describes the presidential center as “a place of dreaming,” and indeed, the Obama museum follows the tautological logic of a labyrinthine Escher staircase endlessly looping upward. Organizers of the past inspired Obama to become an organizer himself, and the people he met along the way inspired him to run for office, where he could inspire the public to elect him, who then inspired Obama to fight for them as president, who built a museum to inspire the public to take action yet again.

This gives the museum’s anecdotes of public service a flat quality — all they are allowed to do is inspire. On touch screens throughout the building, you can see examples of ordinary people who participated in civic action, from abolishing a luxury tax on sanitary products in the UK to giving legal land titles to indigenous people in the Colombian Caribbean. The museum doesn’t say whether these efforts were insurgent or conciliatory, nor what kind of setbacks they faced or how communities responded, just as it does not dwell on the specifics of Obama’s campaigns as an organizer, the movements of the past that inspired him, or the troubles of his presidency.

At the center’s opening ceremony, Obama remarked that his museum “won’t just be an exercise in nostalgia or looking backwards. We want to look forward.” But one cannot create a museum about something that has not happened yet, any more than one can create a top-down grassroots organization, a People’s Organization without the people.

entry.summary: The Barack Obama Presidential Center promised to be more than an ode to the former president. In reality, it’s an $850 million monument to the vacuousness that defined Obama liberalism.

entry.title: Ireland’s Matches Against Israel Should Have Been Canceled

div.p: On Sunday night, the Irish soccer team bowed their heads in silence as the Israeli anthem echoed through the all but empty Nagyerdei Stadium in Debrecen, Hungary’s second-largest city. The Irish players, who wore black armbands, skipped the traditional pregame rituals. There were no handshakes, no pennants, and (for the most part) no fans.

After months of deliberations and growing demands for a boycott, these trite gestures of dissent were all the Irish team could muster. Having spurned an opportunity to set an international precedent, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) succumbed to fear, meekly agreeing to go through with the matches.

This was a decision that the Irish players had seemed destined to glumly accept until some final deliberations nearly scuttled the ship at the eleventh hour. In the end, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu opted to take a one-man stand after a truly dramatic day for Irish soccer.

The evolution of this match into a contentious diplomatic high-wire act demonstrates the full extent of Israel’s international isolation. Nonetheless, the saga ultimately reveals how, despite ardent public support, fears of punitive action continue to undermine Irish support for Palestine.

Israel selected Hungary as the location of its Nations League clash against Ireland, the site of nearly all its “home” internationals since October 7, 2023. Although the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) did not allocate away tickets for Irish fans, a dozen or so diehards managed to enter the stadium to offer their support.

Not only were Irish fans effectively blocked from attending, but the national broadcaster, Raidió Teilifís Éireann (RTÉ), also decided to strip back its coverage to the bare minimum. Television viewership dropped below its usual levels as fans across the country staged mini-boycotts of their own.

The shrill blast of the opening whistle ultimately brought down the curtain on a failed boycott campaign that had gripped the country for months. At this late stage, the very fact that the game was even happening seemed to overshadow the importance of its actual outcome.

At the end of an admittedly challenging week, Ireland took out their frustration on their opponents from the start, amassing a three–nil lead in the space of just twenty-five minutes. After scoring Ireland’s third and final goal, Jack Moylan removed his black armband and kissed it in front of the Israeli fans in an apparent gesture of Palestinian solidarity.

No number of goals or pointed celebrations could dampen the spirit of the hundred or so Israeli fans who had made the pilgrimage to Hungary. Regardless of the result, they seemed to be celebrating the mere fact that the game had gone ahead.

Even after their team had gone three goals down, the Israeli supporters continued to chant in support of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF). In a video recorded from the stands, Yoseph Haddad, a far-right Israeli activist, proclaimed that while Ireland might have won, “they will never, ever break the Israeli spirit.”

The Israeli fans reportedly directed racist abuse at one of Ireland’s goal scorers, Adam Idah. UEFA have since declined to investigate the incident on the basis that the Irish players did not properly report it. This appears to mean that while Idah’s teammate Jayson Molumby asked the match officials to listen to the chanting, he did not specifically mention the word “racism.”
As the game wore on, tempers frayed. Various on-field scuffles later culminated in an alleged changing room melee between Irish defender Jake O’Brien and Israeli captain Manor Solomon.

The hostility continued well after the final whistle. In a post-match outburst, Solomon boasted to reporters that “we have a country that is ten times better than theirs.” When asked about the Irish players, the former IDF soldier said that he would probably be suspended if he stated his opinion in full: “Obviously they hate us, and we don’t like them.”

Ireland, who have not won a competitive game by this margin in over three years, sliced through the Israeli defense with uncharacteristic precision. Any satisfaction came with a nagging sense of guilt, knowing that any victory pales in comparison to what could have been gained by a full-fledged boycott.

As soon as UEFA announced the Nations League draw back in February, many Irish fans mobilized behind the boycott campaign. On the eve of Sunday’s game, over 160 Irish sports figures had signed an open letter urging the team to stop the game.

With public pressure mounting, the FAI opted to play Ireland’s second game against Israel, which was due to take place in Dublin, at a small stadium in rural Serbia instead, citing “security concerns” as a rationale. The FAI’s decision essentially denied Irish fans the chance to directly picket any of the games.

Within the Irish football community, the debate has created a rift between the grassroots and those at the institutional level. A broad coalition of fans, players, and coaches from the domestic league has come out strongly against the FAI’s decision.

The FAI officials responsible for the decision to play seemed keen to avoid the spotlight and left the team’s Icelandic head coach, Heimir Hallgrímson, to bear the brunt of public scrutiny. The Israel Football Association launched an extraordinary attack on Hallgrímson after he made the following statement in the run-up to the game: “We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide. We are playing against Israel; we are not playing with Israel.”
There can be few if any precedents in modern sporting history for the Israel FA’s official response:

blockquote.p: We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way. Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by the Republic of Ireland team coach. We’re not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we’re playing against the coach who embodies them.

div.p: This put paid to any notion that it was possible to keep politics out of sport in this situation. However, the FAI did not see it as an opportunity to revisit their decision to play the games.

Nor did they see any need to publicly defend Hallgrímson. The Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, did intervene on his behalf, branding the Israeli remarks “unacceptable” and calling for them to be withdrawn: “Israel can’t keep denying what the world knows, and what the world understands.” But there was no statement from the FAI, although it was reported to have complained to UEFA privately.

The FAI could easily have stated that Hallgrímson was using the word “genocide” because this is the official position of the Irish government, which has decided to join the South African case at the International Court of Justice, accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention through its actions in Gaza. It could also have briefed Hallgrímson to make the same point in his defense. There appears to have been no effort to do so.

Ill-equipped to handle the political weight of the situation, the former dentist wilted in the line of fire at the pre-match press conference. Hallgrímson fielded questions from combative Israeli journalists, hounding him over a past coaching position in Qatar as well as Ireland’s decision to play against Nazi Germany in the 1930s. Under pressure, he apologized for using the word “genocide” in his previous statement: “It is a strong word and the wrong word for me to use.”

Hallgrímson’s capitulation seemed only to embolden the Israel FA, which flippantly declared, after Ireland agreed to play, that “football had won.” Israel FA Head of Communications Shlomi Barzel was asked if he was responsible for the statement that charged Hallgrímson with “stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy.” His response was defiant: “I am responsible for that, and I am not going to apologize. After hearing him today, I will take back the word ‘stupidity.’” In other words, he stood by his description of the Ireland manager as an ignorant hypocrite.

With most of the public discontent directed at both the FAI and the Irish government, recent protests had started to target the players themselves. Activists had picketed the team’s Dublin hotel before they departed for their upcoming games.

After the team suffered an ignominious defeat to Kosovo a few days beforehand, Irish midfielder Jason Knight became the first player to state that the games against Israel should not go ahead. Others, such as Chiedozie Ogbene, later vented their frustration, urging the public “not to put pressure on us.”
As uncertainty spread through the camp, news broke on Saturday that goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu would be withdrawing from the match-day squad. He issued a statement explaining his motivations:

blockquote.p: My decision is based purely upon my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong. It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community but against the atrocities in the region. There are few times where you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger and I strongly believe this is one of them.

div.p: Reporters camped outside the hotel as Irish players deliberated on whether to go ahead with the game.

Former Ireland manager Brian Kerr, who has been a vocal supporter of the boycott campaign, was in touch with Bazunu. He reported that a vote was held with Bazunu absent, with the players voting 14–8 in favor of going ahead. The FAI declined to confirm or deny the exact figures, merely referring to a “significant majority” among the players.

Having had months to establish a firm stance, the FAI haplessly equivocated. According to Brian Kerr, Bazunu was left “feeling quite low and shunned by some of the players and by the FAI” after his decision.

Seemingly immune to the chorus of criticism, FAI President Paul Cooke later claimed that the situation “went as well as could be expected in the face of unprecedented coverage.” Opposition parties have since called on the FAI leadership to step down in the wake of the fiasco.

The FAI cited the threat of disciplinary action in support of its decision not to boycott the matches. The decision also comes against the backdrop of Ireland cohosting the 2028 European Championship — the country’s first time staging a major tournament.

In a bulletin distributed to FAI members at a July extraordinary general meeting (EGM), the association suggested that Ireland could be suspended from future competitions in the event of a boycott. Further estimations of a potential $10.3 million loss of revenue seem overblown in the light of other recent boycott actions.

Since 2024, Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia have all refused to play various women’s and underage matches against Belarus, citing the country’s ongoing involvement in the Ukraine war. UEFA docked the Baltic teams no more than three points each, and in one instance dished out a €5,000 fine.

After the match on Sunday, the FAI’s Paul Cooke referred to the exclusion of Southampton from the promotion playoffs for the English Championship earlier this year as an example of what might have happened to Ireland in the event of a boycott. But the two situations could hardly be less similar: Southampton were punished for spying on the training sessions of their rivals.

The Irish players may have also been subjected to other forms of external pressure. Several well-informed sources passed on rumors that some players were told by their agents that they might be blacklisted from playing for English clubs with American owners if they chose not to play.

Although they rejected the boycott at the July EGM, FAI members voted overwhelmingly last November to submit a motion calling for Israel’s suspension from UEFA. This obvious contradiction demonstrates how institutional support for Palestine does not yet outweigh the perceived costs of unilateral action.

Under similar circumstances in 1999, Ireland chose to boycott a European qualifier against Yugoslavia because of atrocities carried out in Kosovo. The FAI avoided expulsion from the European Championship, receiving only a moderate fine from UEFA.

Norway, which hosted Israel in a World Cup qualifier earlier last year, has spearheaded the campaign to suspend Israel from UEFA. Its officials have drawn comparisons with the ban on Russian national and club teams that UEFA imposed soon after the invasion of Ukraine began.

Following the recent controversy, the FAI asked that Ireland and Israel be separated from future group stage pairings. UEFA denied the request on the basis that the two nations “have never been in direct conflict.”

The ongoing controversy has unfolded against the backdrop of Ireland’s increasingly strained relations with Israel. The Irish government has imposed travel bans on two far-right Israeli ministers and recently moved to prohibit the import of goods from Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territories.

Ireland’s heavy reliance on US investment leaves it potentially vulnerable to pressure from Washington. Before his recent death, Republican Senator Lindsey Graham threatened that countries that “participate in the effort to marginalize Israel in sports” would “pay a heavy price when it comes to access to the American economy.”

The Occupied Territories Bill had promised to be a groundbreaking piece of legislation when first proposed to the Irish parliament in 2018. After extensive deliberations, the government eventually passed a diluted version of the bill earlier this year, which excluded trade in services from the ban.

Despite otherwise advocating for international sanctions on Israel, the Irish government has supported the FAI’s decision to participate in the games. “We don’t want to damage ourselves unnecessarily,” cautioned Micheál Martin. In a separate interview, he argued that “sport is an area that can be challenging when it crosses into the realm of politics.”

Martin’s comments echo the rhetoric of international soccer bodies that extol the sport’s power to unite people while approaching contentious political issues with caution if not cowardice. Amid demands for Israel’s suspension, FIFA President Gianni Infantino has said that “football cannot solve geopolitical problems,” instead summoning its “power to bring people together in a divided world.”

At FIFA’s annual congress this year, Infantino tried to organize a now infamous photo op between Israeli and Palestinian delegates. The toe-curling gaffe followed a passionate speech by the Palestinian representative in which he called for sanctions against Israel over the formation of soccer clubs in the occupied territories.

Although the decisive nature of the victory may have restored some public faith in the team, it remains to be seen how the fans will receive the players when they take on Austria in Dublin today. The match comes just days before the second clash against Israel in Serbia.

The FAI has already moved fans with pitch-side seats in anticipation of further protest action. Ireland’s last home game, a May friendly against Qatar, featured a demonstration in which fans threw tennis balls with printed Palestine flags onto the pitch.

In what briefly promised to be the dawn of a new era in the global campaign to boycott Israel, the limits of Irish institutional support for Palestine have become clear. Without coordinated multilateral action involving other associations, the FAI seems unlikely to lead by example, particularly under its current gutless leadership.

Despite the best efforts of those leaders to isolate sports from politics, this contentious match proves that the two are inseparable, if not integral to each other. With the FAI’s credibility all but erased, it’s left to the players once again to make a decision.

entry.summary: Irish goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu took a brave stand by refusing to play against Israel on Sunday night. It was the cowardice of football’s governing bodies and their refusal to exclude Israel from international competition that made his stand necessary.

entry.title: Frederick Douglass Had a Radical Respect for the Constitution

div.p: Is the US Constitution for or against slavery? Questions concerning the legacy of America’s founding and how to interpret the Constitution have long gripped public discourse; in recent years they have become inseparable. From the 1980s came the originalists, a group of legal theorists who sought to recover the Constitution’s original meaning through textual analysis buttressed by historical investigation. Adhering to the document’s original meaning, they argue, promotes institutional stability and the rule of law.

Scholars have long contested these claims, challenging the plausibility of recovering an “original meaning” or doubting the authoritative nature of such meaning even if discovered. Recently, however, a second phenomenon has brought constitutional discourse closer to political discourse. The 1619 Project has inspired new attacks against the originalist normative claim, as it recasts the nation’s history in terms of its legacy as a slaveholding nation committed to white supremacy. Scholars are now challenging originalism on the grounds that it is part and parcel of a tradition of oppression that cannot demand a people’s loyalty, much less respect.

This reframes the question from the accessibility of original meaning and its authoritative nature to the problem of original meaning as it relates to constitutional evils. Still, originalists continue to defend the founding of the United States as a moment that instilled constitutional norms worth preserving. Indeed, they are compelled to do so. Originalism would not be worth its salt — promoting stability and the rule of law — if it meant only preserving oppression and white supremacy. Increasingly, we find two historical accounts representing two mutually exclusive Americas: an America founded on perpetuating slavery and white supremacy versus an America dedicated to liberty and equality.

This clash of narratives is hardly new. The antebellum period was rife with political disputes concerning the future of slavery. Proslavery and antislavery advocates alike turned to the past to measure America as it was against what it should be. Slavery’s defenders argued that the institution was a positive good and that the framers of the Constitution enshrined protections for it. Fidelity to the founding of the nation, in their view, required protecting slavery as an indispensable American institution. Antislavery advocates, alternatively, argued that the Constitution did not recognize slavery as a positive good but set it on a course for eventual extinction.

Defenders of slavery and antislavery advocates used conflicting interpretive frameworks to justify their respective understandings of the Constitution’s treatment of slavery. As is the case in the present day, both narratives posited conflicting accounts concerning history and its authoritative grip on the present. Still, both sides recognized that, at some level, one could not chart a course for a future that had no regard for the debt owed to the past.

There is one figure in history who is uniquely positioned to shed light on complex nineteenth-century constitutional development and to speak to our current constitutional-political moment: Frederick Douglass, the former slave turned radical activist turned statesman.

Modern-day critics and proponents of the Constitution’s beginnings alike reference the controversial conclusion in his famous speech “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” that the Constitution was a “GLORIOUS LIBERTY DOCUMENT.” In that speech, Douglass has many rhetorical flourishes that either side might find useful in vindicating its position on the Constitution. Those who seek to salvage the Constitution from its relationship with slavery hold Douglass up as paradigmatic of proper veneration of the Constitution. Those who seek to malign the Constitution’s beginnings tend to focus on his scathing rebuke of America — in the very same speech — as his true message. Any reference to the Constitution or the Founders in positive terms, they argue, is nothing more than a rhetorical device aimed at increasing the potency of Douglass’s censure of the nation.

But both groups fail to seriously consider the method behind his conclusion. What both accounts miss is that Douglass has much more to offer concerning constitutional fidelity and constitutional interpretation than his “Fourth of July” speech. Constitutional fidelity is not to be blindly adhered to; nor is it merely a pragmatic consideration. The Constitution is truly good when correctly interpreted.

Douglass’s constitutional thought uniquely answered the question of what the Constitution’s posture toward slavery was. While some abolitionists simply accepted slavery as an indelible blemish on the Constitution, Douglass sought to redeem the Constitution from the evils of slavery. Indeed, he helped constitutional abolitionists popularize a natural rights theory of interpretation that excised slavery from the Constitution. Through this interpretation, he sought to put all persons on equal footing before the law. His great task, as he described it, was “by voice and pen . . . to stand for the freedom of people of all colors, until in our land the last yoke was broken and the last bondsman was set free.” His approach to the Constitution was critical in that endeavor, and it contributed to burgeoning constitutional thought in the antebellum period.

Douglass was a cardinal figure during one of the most consequential moments in US constitutional development. He was a direct participant in the antebellum debate over slavery, which set in motion several theories of constitutional interpretation. Though methods and conclusions varied, each side of the debate claimed fidelity to the Constitution through an appeal to its text and to history. These debates shaped constitutional thought during the antebellum period and carried over into public deliberation during Reconstruction.

Among the throng of opinions, we find Douglass arguing that based on the text, history, and natural rights, the Constitution was resolutely antislavery. His method was based primarily on natural rights principles. He argued that the Founders built this nation on a natural rights foundation, the principles of which were pronounced in the Declaration of Independence. As such, one had to interpret the Constitution according to those natural rights principles.

But studying Douglass provides more than an arresting theory of constitutional interpretation. His intellectual journey is fascinating: he discovered for himself the significance of the nation’s founding principles after having survived harrowing experiences of cruelty and oppression under the color of law. Insufficient attention is given to just how exceptional Douglass was. After he escaped to freedom, he ventured into the world of the antislavery movement. There he quickly found fellowship with William Lloyd Garrison, an experience-hardened abolitionist who famously referred to the Constitution as “a covenant with death, and an agreement with hell.” Garrison and his camp, relying on James Madison’s Notes of Debates in the Federal Convention of 1787, argued incessantly that the Constitution was irredeemably a proslavery document and that the Union, by extension, was a curse. This left the Garrisonians only one possibility: the abolition of slavery meant disunion and abolishing the Constitution along with it.

At first, Douglass adopted these views without reservation; he spoke at antislavery conventions across the North, disparaging the framers, cursing the founding, and expressing nothing but contempt for the Constitution. Douglass’s inquisitive and capacious mind could not long be satisfied with received wisdom, however. In a short time, he abandoned the Garrisonian position. As he consulted more accounts of the founding and the Constitution, Douglass became convinced that the Constitution was in fact an antislavery document, and that the truest interpretation of it would require abolishing slavery for the sake of union. Most look to him for his exceptional oratory skills, which have withstood the test of time, and rightfully so. Yet lurking under his witty remarks and fierce retorts attacking the power of the slave-owning class rested a cogent theory of law and legal interpretation.

Douglass also offers a lesson for political actors who must confront the tension between their own theories and the demands of politics. Rarely does history provide an example of a figure with an intellectual stature comparable to Douglass and place that figure at the center of great constitutional change. He had a robust theory of law and justice that guided his actions during the antebellum period. It was only during Reconstruction, however, that political realities forced Douglass to act in ways that did not always reflect his theory. Douglass believed that the United States would be “complete” only when it granted equal rights to all its citizens, and especially universal suffrage.

At the time, this meant expanding the circle of democratic participation to African Americans and women. But after early defeats in Reconstruction, it became clear to Douglass that there was insufficient political will to extend suffrage to both groups. Douglass’s natural rights constitutionalism had a clear answer for what the nation needed to do, but ideas alone could not bring a constitutional amendment into being. Confronted with the political exigencies of Reconstruction, Douglass pushed for African American suffrage at the expense of women’s suffrage to move the arc of justice forward. Douglass calculated the move to be an unfortunate but necessary one. As soon as the Fifteenth Amendment — which guaranteed suffrage regardless of race — was ratified, Douglass went to work again in favor of women’s suffrage. Indeed, he proves an excellent exemplar of the timeless question of prudence when confronted with this tension between theory and practice.

For these reasons, Douglass remains relevant for Americans today. He teaches us much about our past and how to confront it in a sober but hopeful way. He also teaches us something of what it means to traverse adversity for the sake of justice, and how it at times might require momentary sacrifice for long-term gains. Douglass preserves the legacy of the Constitution in favor of freedom and provides a method for ensuring the Constitution delivers a brighter tomorrow.

entry.summary: Frederick Douglass believed the US would only live up to its ideals when it granted equal rights to all citizens. He thought the best way to do this was to show that the Constitution was a radical document capable of delivering on this promise.

entry.title: Democrats Have Created a Consultant-Driven Echo Chamber

div.p: “The number one rule of political fundraising,” Evan Barker writes in the first line of Nothing Left: Confessions of a Democratic Operative, “is to never, ever, under any circumstances, speak about it publicly.” Then she spends 288 pages talking about it, and it’s a wonderful thing that she does.

Barker’s insider account of her time deep in the bowels of the Democratic Party often reads like The Jungle of Democratic fundraising: Upton Sinclair showed readers how the sausage got made, and Barker shows how the candidates do. By the end, it’s clear that the Democrats are a glorified fundraising organization with an electoral department attached, one that absorbs idealism, monetizes it, and then disciplines anyone who threatens its arrangements, often with the cynical deployment of identity politics.

Some of the book’s most compelling sections are autobiography. At times, it’s like Hillbilly Elegy but one that wears a blue lanyard. Like J. D. Vance, Barker is a striver from the hollowed-out middle of the country. In her case, that’s Missouri, where her mother and grandmother live on Social Security checks and the towns feel, as she puts it, “stripped for parts and left behind.” At seventeen, she was cutting class to intern for Barack Obama in Kansas City, running phone banks for volunteers three times her age.

For Barker, politics was a matter of life and death in the most literal sense — she has a rare genetic lung disease. Insurers could reject her because of a preexisting condition, and her parents could not simply buy their way around the problem. “My disease will kill me if I can’t get insurance after high school,” she told the law students she trained to register voters, and a version of her story later turned up in a Michelle Obama speech.

header.h2: Barker Joined the Dems for All the Right Reasons

div.p: It’s an interesting paradox: Barker joined the Democrats because she believed they could turn a private struggle into a collective solution, but her career reveals a party that’s much better at turning that struggle into a fundraising pitch. The book follows her journey as she climbs the ladder: Brent Welder’s Bernie Sanders–backed 2018 primary campaign in Kansas’s Third District, then Adam Green’s Progressive Change Campaign Committee, and finally Left Rising, a progressive consultancy.

Barker’s specialty was “call time,” the hours-a-day ritual in which fundraisers artfully beg rich people for money. Along the way, she found an unlikely professional inspiration: Alec Baldwin’s character in Glengarry Glen Ross, the motivational sadist who browbeats salesmen into following his personal mantra: “ABC — Always Be Closing.” Left Rising’s ambition was to “professionalize” the Left, equipping insurgents with the skills to navigate the corrupt political system their establishment opponents already knew. This strategy had obvious logic: candidates cannot win on righteous intentions alone. But professionalization also brought the insurgency deeper into the world it hoped to overturn.

Through Barker’s career, we peer behind the curtain and watch political candidates, many handpicked by the establishment, learn the art of being a Democrat in the 2010s. This was the decade both parties got taken over. Donald Trump seized the GOP like a casino he’d leveraged to the hilt. The Democrats were captured by something softer: they tried to keep perpetuating incremental Clinton- and Obama-era politics while adopting the vocabulary of a humanities seminar/HR department.

The machine’s main job was keeping the Bernie wing out. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) blacklisted any consultant who worked for a primary challenger, and Barker says she ended up on the list. EMILYs List, which she argues cares about little except money, lined up early behind the establishment candidate, Sharice Davids, against Welder. In Omaha, in 2018, the House Majority PAC pulled its money out of left-populist Kara Eastman’s winnable race in the home stretch, and she lost to the Republican. Barker is convinced that the Third Way and the establishment preferred this outcome, even if it meant handing a seat to the GOP. In Texas, she claims that the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) helped plant a spoiler candidate to drain Latino votes from Cristina Tzintzún Ramírez’s Senate primary. And in an election twist that Jacobin readers are no doubt familiar with, Elizabeth Warren smeared Bernie as a sexist on a debate stage in 2020. Barker is less successful with her half-hearted criticisms of the Bernie left (if the insurgents are too pure and the establishment is bought, where exactly is a left-winger supposed to go?) and the man himself, who has the gall to ask for his water bottles at rallies to be stripped of their labels — how dare he!

Many of Barker’s other observations and behind-the-scenes details ring as grimly funny. Her working theory is that politicians are often high-functioning psychopaths, and she teaches trainees a taxonomy of candidate types. Gavin Newsom is “The Machine.” Jasmine Crockett is “The Influencer,” convinced she’ll go viral and raise millions — no matter where those millions come from (the crypto industry, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee). Last on the list comes “The Lost Cause,” which is “regular people who are running for the right reasons but who lack the ruthlessness required to fundraise.” Her example: “No one you’ve ever heard of.”

Fittingly, Barker eventually ends up at a fundraiser in Alec Baldwin’s New York home, surrounded by portraits of Civil War generals and a jelly bean tower. Baldwin, gruff in public, turns out to be warm and curious in private, asking Barker where she’s from. He may be the most likable figure in the book.

header.h2: How “the Race-Class Narrative” Dooms the Dems

div.p: But it’s not all bad. Early in the Biden years, Barker describes a moment of hope, when the Democratic Party seemed to have learned something from the Bernie campaigns. There were stimulus checks, an expanded child tax credit that cut child poverty nearly in half, and a Build Back Better agenda that was the closest the Democrats had come to embracing material politics in a generation.

Then the child tax credit lapsed, and Joe Manchin killed Build Back Better. The party’s energy went instead into what Barker calls “RCN” (the Race-Class Narrative), a framework in which every economic demand had to justify itself in racial, rather than universal, terms. She recounts one Zoom call that raised almost half a million dollars for outreach to “the LatinX community,” with Christine Pelosi — Nancy’s daughter — among the donors.

She also describes a bleak working environment after 2020 in which “life became a virtue-signaling contest between me and other white operatives.” If you couldn’t sh-t-talk white men or self-flagellate about your white woman privilege in Dem World, you were playing the game wrong. After Bernie lost, Barker observes, universal health care went from the primary issue to a secondary one as “identity politics and social justice issues were a good distraction for us all.” But health care is what brought Barker into the belly of the Democratic Party beast in the first place.

By the time she reaches the 2024 Democratic National Convention (DNC), when she’s surrounded by goofy chants of “joy” and “Brat Summer” while her mother and grandmother struggle with grocery bills back home, she cracks. A woman with a camera asks her to name her favorite Kamala Harris policy, and Barker’s mind goes blank. She walks out partway through the convention and, as her book’s title suggests, finds there is nothing left for her at the DNC.

The problem is that somewhere along the way, Barker gets red-pilled. The podcast Red Scare becomes her secret refuge (“Finally, I had friends to laugh with at the dumb politicians I was helping elect”), and after the convention she sits for a friendly interview with Lara Trump. Then she votes for Donald Trump. She presents the vote as revenge, a middle finger to the people who burned her. But the two years since have not been kind to the politics of “F-ck you.” The Republican mega-bill Trump signed in July 2025 made the deepest cuts to Medicaid in the program’s history; the Congressional Budget Office projects the bill will leave around ten million more Americans uninsured. For someone whose political awakening began with a preexisting condition, it’s a strange way to get even.
To modify a line from Glengarry Glen Ross, Barker was right that the Democrats’ leads were weak. Her mistake was taking them to Trump.
